text: This painting hangs in the Louvre behind protective glass. It was painted with a hazy technique called sfumato, and its sitter is traditionally identified as Lisa Gherardini. The sitter's enigmatic smile has fascinated viewers for centuries. For 10 points, name this portrait by Leonardo da Vinci.

This artist painted The Starry Night while staying at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. He applied paint in thick, swirling strokes and painted several canvases of sunflowers. He famously cut off part of his own ear. For 10 points, name this Dutch Post-Impressionist.

This artist's Blue Period came after the suicide of his friend Carlos Casagemas. He painted a huge black-and-white mural about the bombing of a Basque town and the Spanish Civil War. He also painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon. For 10 points, name this Spanish painter who worked in Paris.

This artist painted a ceiling in the Vatican with scenes from the Book of Genesis, including The Creation of Adam. He lay on scaffolding for years to finish it, and also carved the Pietà. For 10 points, name this Italian artist of the Sistine Chapel.

This painter's Persistence of Memory shows soft melting watches in a barren landscape. He was known for his upturned waxed mustache and his dreamlike imagery. He was born in Figueres, in Catalonia. For 10 points, name this Spanish painter.

This artist made silkscreen prints of Campbell's Soup cans and of Marilyn Monroe. He ran a New York studio called the Factory. He said everyone would be famous for fifteen minutes. For 10 points, name this leading figure of pop art.

This painter is known for her many self-portraits, such as The Two Fridas, which often show her thick eyebrows. She lived in a blue house in Coyoacán in Mexico City. She was married to a famous muralist. For 10 points, name this Mexican painter.

This artist dripped and poured paint onto huge canvases laid on the floor. His method was called action painting, and his works include Lavender Mist and Autumn Rhythm. He worked in Springs, New York. For 10 points, name this American Abstract Expressionist.

This art movement is named after a hazy Claude Monet seascape of a sunrise. Its painters, including Renoir and Degas, captured fleeting effects of light, often painting outdoors. They used short, visible brushstrokes. For 10 points, name this nineteenth-century French art movement.

This Dutch Golden Age painter made dozens of self-portraits throughout his life. His group portrait of a militia company, The Night Watch, is in the Rijksmuseum. He was a master of dramatic light and shadow. For 10 points, name this artist of The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Tulp.

This painter lived in Delft and made small, quiet interior scenes lit by a window, such as The Milkmaid. He also painted a portrait of a girl wearing a blue and yellow turban. For 10 points, name this Dutch artist of Girl with a Pearl Earring.

This Florentine painter showed a nude goddess standing on a giant scallop shell in a painting for the Medici family. He also painted Primavera. For 10 points, name this Italian Renaissance artist of The Birth of Venus.

This painter's most famous work shows a stern farmer holding a pitchfork beside a woman in front of a white house with a pointed window. The models were his dentist and his sister. For 10 points, name this Iowa artist of American Gothic.

This artist painted close-up views of flowers, as well as bleached animal skulls against the desert sky. She spent her later years in New Mexico, near Ghost Ranch. For 10 points, name this American painter of Black Iris.

This mural was painted on a refectory wall of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. It shows twelve men reacting as their leader announces that one of them will betray him. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci painting of Jesus and his apostles.

This French artist led the Fauves, whose paintings use bright, wild colors. Late in life, he made cut-paper collages such as The Snail. His works include The Dance and The Red Studio. For 10 points, name this French painter.

This American painter depicted lonely figures in a late-night diner in a work titled Nighthawks. He also painted Early Sunday Morning and House by the Railroad. His paintings capture urban isolation. For 10 points, name this realist painter.

This statue stands over seventeen feet tall in the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence. It was carved from a single block of marble by Michelangelo and shows a young shepherd before a battle with a giant. For 10 points, name this statue of a biblical hero.
This French sculptor made a bronze of a nude man sitting with his chin on his fist, The Thinker. He also carved The Kiss and made the Gates of Hell. For 10 points, name this sculptor.

Georges Seurat's A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte is a famous example of this technique. Paul Signac also used it, placing small dots of pure color side by side so they blend in the viewer's eye. For 10 points, name this painting technique that uses tiny dots.

This American artist moved to Paris, where she exhibited with Edgar Degas and the Impressionists. She painted tender scenes of mothers and children, such as The Child's Bath. For 10 points, name this woman who painted The Boating Party.

This American illustrator painted many covers for The Saturday Evening Post. His series Four Freedoms includes Freedom from Want, a Thanksgiving scene. His Rosie the Riveter was a cover from 1943. For 10 points, name this artist.

This Japanese artist's woodblock print shows a huge curling wave about to swamp fishing boats, with a small Mount Fuji in the distance. It is part of his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. For 10 points, name this ukiyo-e artist of The Great Wave off Kanagawa.

This Mexican artist painted the Detroit Industry murals. His mural for Rockefeller Center was destroyed after he included a portrait of Lenin. He painted giant murals at the National Palace in Mexico City. For 10 points, name this muralist.

This word means "rebirth" in French. This period began in Florence in the fourteenth century and produced artists like Raphael and Leonardo. It revived interest in the art of ancient Greece and Rome. For 10 points, give this term for the era that followed the Middle Ages in Europe.

Painters traditionally say that these colors cannot be made by mixing other colors. Mixing two of them produces colors like orange and green. They are red, yellow, and blue. For 10 points, name this set of three basic colors.

Georges Braque and the painter of Guernica worked together on this style, which has analytic and synthetic phases. Its paintings break objects into geometric shapes and show them from several viewpoints at once. For 10 points, name this twentieth-century art movement.

This painting medium uses pigments mixed with water, and the paint is applied to paper in thin, transparent layers. The paper shows through, and white areas are usually left unpainted. For 10 points, name this medium used by Winslow Homer and John Singer Sargent.

The Sistine Chapel ceiling was made using this method, in which artists paint on wet plaster so that the pigment becomes part of the wall. Its name is Italian for "fresh." For 10 points, name this mural technique.

This Italian polymath drew the Vitruvian Man and filled notebooks with designs for flying machines. He painted The Virgin of the Rocks and was born in the town of Vinci. His notebooks were written in mirror script. For 10 points, name this Renaissance artist of the Mona Lisa.

text: This composer kept writing music after going deaf. He wrote nine symphonies, including one whose last movement sets Schiller's Ode to Joy. He also wrote the Moonlight Sonata. For 10 points, name this German composer of the Fifth Symphony.

This composer was a child prodigy who toured Europe with his sister Nannerl. He lived in Vienna and wrote The Marriage of Figaro and The Magic Flute. He wrote the Requiem, which was left unfinished. For 10 points, name this Austrian composer.

This composer worked as a church musician in Leipzig. He wrote six Brandenburg Concertos and The Well-Tempered Clavier. He was a master of the fugue and had many musical children. For 10 points, name this German Baroque composer.

This instrument has four strings tuned to G, D, A, and E and is played with a horsehair bow. It is the highest-pitched string instrument in the orchestra's string section. Antonio Stradivari made famous ones in Cremona. For 10 points, name this instrument.

This instrument was invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori in Italy around 1700. Pressing a key makes a felt hammer strike a string. A standard one has 88 keys. For 10 points, name this keyboard instrument.

This Italian term, abbreviated with the letter f in sheet music, tells the performer to play loudly. Its opposite is piano, and its stronger version is fortissimo. Composers write these dynamic markings below the staff. For 10 points, give this musical dynamic marking.
This Russian composer wrote the ballets Swan Lake and The Nutcracker. His 1812 Overture ends with cannon fire. His Sixth Symphony is called the Pathétique. For 10 points, name this Romantic composer.

This Baroque composer wrote four violin concertos named for the seasons. Born in Venice, he worked at a school for orphaned girls, the Ospedale della Pietà, and was a priest with red hair. He wrote hundreds of concertos and the oratorio Juditha triumphans. For 10 points, name this Baroque composer of The Four Seasons.

This band from Liverpool included John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr. Its albums include Abbey Road and Sergeant Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band. For 10 points, name this British rock band of "Hey Jude."

This New Orleans trumpeter was nicknamed Satchmo. He sang with a gravelly voice on "What a Wonderful World" and led groups called the Hot Five and the Hot Seven. For 10 points, name this jazz musician.

This person stands on a podium in front of an orchestra and uses a baton to keep time. This person also controls the tempo and shapes the interpretation of the music. For 10 points, name this leader of an orchestra or choir.
This art form is Italian for "work," and combines singing, an orchestra, costumes, and acting on stage. La Traviata and Carmen are examples. For 10 points, name this form of musical drama.
This German composer wrote Hungarian Dances and a famous lullaby beginning "Guten Abend, gut' Nacht." He wrote four symphonies and a German Requiem. For 10 points, name this Romantic composer.

This American composer wrote Rhapsody in Blue and the opera Porgy and Bess. His orchestral work An American in Paris includes taxi horns. His brother Ira wrote lyrics. For 10 points, name this composer.

This composer died at age thirty-one after writing hundreds of songs. His Unfinished Symphony has only two completed movements. He also set Goethe's poem Erlkönig to music. For 10 points, name this Viennese composer of Winterreise.

This Polish composer wrote mostly for solo piano, including nocturnes, waltzes, polonaises, and mazurkas. He moved to Paris and had a relationship with the writer George Sand. For 10 points, name this Romantic pianist.

This is the largest ensemble form in classical music, usually in four movements and played by a full orchestra. Haydn wrote more than one hundred of them. For 10 points, give this term for a long orchestral work.

This American genre grew out of New Orleans and relies on improvisation and syncopated rhythms. Swing, bebop, and Dixieland are types. For 10 points, name this genre played by Duke Ellington and Miles Davis.

This composer wrote the ballets Petrushka and The Firebird for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes. He was born in Russia but later became an American citizen. His pulsing, dissonant 1913 ballet about a pagan sacrifice caused a scandal in Paris. For 10 points, name this Russian-born composer.

This American composer wrote the ballet Appalachian Spring and Fanfare for the Common Man. His music uses open harmonies and folk tunes. He also wrote the ballet Rodeo. For 10 points, name this composer.
This French composer wrote Clair de lune and La mer. He also wrote Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun. His music is associated with Impressionism. For 10 points, name this composer.
This woodwind instrument has no reed. The player blows across a hole near one end, and the instrument is held sideways. The piccolo is a smaller relative. For 10 points, name this instrument.

This Austrian composer, nicknamed "Papa," wrote the Surprise Symphony and the Farewell Symphony. He spent years working for the Esterházy family and taught Beethoven. For 10 points, name this composer.
This oratorio by George Frideric Handel premiered in Dublin in 1742. Audiences traditionally stand during its Hallelujah chorus. For 10 points, name this oratorio about the life of Christ.

This singer was born in Tupelo, Mississippi, and rose to fame at Sun Records in Memphis. Known as the King of Rock and Roll, he recorded "Hound Dog" and "Jailhouse Rock" and lived at Graceland. For 10 points, name this American singer.

At the beginning of a line of sheet music, this symbol shows which pitches the lines and spaces stand for. The G one swirls around the second line of the staff. For 10 points, name this symbol, such as treble or bass.
Timpani, snare drums, cymbals, and xylophones belong to this family of instruments. They are played by striking, shaking, or scraping. For 10 points, name this section of the orchestra.

This interval spans eight diatonic scale degrees, such as from one C to the next C. The two notes sound very similar because their frequencies are in a ratio of two to one. For 10 points, name this interval.

This German composer built his own opera house in Bayreuth, the Festspielhaus, to stage his works. He wrote The Ring of the Nibelung, which includes The Valkyrie. He used leitmotifs. For 10 points, name this composer.

This brass instrument has three valves and a bright, piercing tone. Louis Armstrong and Miles Davis played it, and it often plays fanfares in orchestras and marching bands. For 10 points, name this high brass instrument.

text: This film series begins with a scrolling yellow text crawl and a ship chased by a huge star destroyer. Its characters include Luke Skywalker, Princess Leia, and Han Solo. Fans say "May the Force be with you." For 10 points, name this space opera created by George Lucas.

This 1939 film begins in black and white in Kansas, then turns to color when the heroine arrives in a magical land. Judy Garland sang "Over the Rainbow" in it. The heroine follows a yellow brick road with a Scarecrow, a Tin Man, and a Cowardly Lion. For 10 points, name this film based on a book by L. Frank Baum.

This man created Mickey Mouse and produced the first full-length cel-animated feature, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. He opened a California theme park in 1955. His studio also produced Cinderella and Bambi. For 10 points, name this American animator.

This director made a movie about a great white shark terrorizing Amity Island. He also directed E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, Jurassic Park, and Schindler's List. He co-founded DreamWorks. For 10 points, name this American filmmaker.

This 1997 film shows a romance between Jack and Rose aboard an ocean liner that strikes an iceberg. It features the song "My Heart Will Go On" sung by Celine Dion. Its stars are Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet. For 10 points, name this James Cameron film.

This British-born director is called the "Master of Suspense." He made Psycho, with its famous shower scene, and Vertigo. He appeared in brief cameos in most of his films. For 10 points, name this director of Rear Window and The Birds.

This 1995 film was the first feature-length movie made entirely with computer animation. It follows a cowboy doll who is jealous when a space ranger action figure becomes his owner Andy's favorite toy. For 10 points, name this Pixar film starring Woody and Buzz Lightyear.

This 1994 Disney film follows a lion cub who flees after his father Mufasa is killed by his uncle Scar. Its songs by Elton John include "Circle of Life," and it features the phrase "Hakuna Matata." For 10 points, name this animated film about Simba.

Orson Welles directed and starred in this 1941 film, which many critics rank among the best ever made. It begins with a dying newspaper magnate whispering the word "Rosebud." The title character is loosely based on William Randolph Hearst. For 10 points, name this film.

This British-born comic actor played a mustached character called the Tramp. He directed and starred in silent films such as The Kid and Modern Times. He cofounded United Artists. For 10 points, name this star of The Gold Rush.

This animated sitcom set in the town of Springfield was created by Matt Groening. Its title family includes Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and Maggie. It premiered as a series on Fox in 1989. For 10 points, name this long-running show.

In this 1942 film, Humphrey Bogart plays Rick Blaine, who runs a nightclub in Morocco. Ingrid Bergman plays Ilsa, and the film includes the line "Here's looking at you, kid." The song "As Time Goes By" is featured. For 10 points, name this classic wartime romance.

This 1939 epic stars Vivien Leigh as Scarlett O'Hara and Clark Gable as Rhett Butler. It is set in Georgia during the Civil War and Reconstruction, and it ends with the line "Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn." For 10 points, name this film based on Margaret Mitchell's novel.

This New Zealand director filmed a trilogy of films based on Tolkien's books about a ring that must be destroyed. The trilogy's final film won eleven Academy Awards in 2004. He later directed a trilogy of films based on The Hobbit. For 10 points, name this director.

This Japanese director made Rashomon, which tells one crime from conflicting viewpoints. His film Seven Samurai inspired the American Western The Magnificent Seven. He often worked with the actor Toshiro Mifune. For 10 points, name this filmmaker of Ran and Yojimbo.

This Japanese director cofounded Studio Ghibli. His films include My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, and Spirited Away, which won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature. For 10 points, name this animator.

These annual honors are given by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. A golden statuette awarded to winners has a nickname that is often used for the prizes themselves. For 10 points, name these awards for film, which include Best Picture.

This long-running children's television show on PBS takes place on a city street and features Big Bird, Elmo, Oscar the Grouch, and Cookie Monster. It premiered in 1969. For 10 points, name this show.

This Soviet director made Battleship Potemkin, which includes a famous massacre on the Odessa Steps. He developed theories about montage, in which editing creates meaning through juxtaposition. For 10 points, name this director of Strike and October.

This director made 2001: A Space Odyssey, with its sentient computer HAL 9000. He also directed Dr. Strangelove, The Shining, and A Clockwork Orange. He was known for perfectionism and long shoots. For 10 points, name this American-born British filmmaker.

Before filming a movie, directors often use this tool, which is a series of drawings that show each shot in order, like a comic strip. Animators also create it to plan scenes. For 10 points, name this planning tool.

In movies, these three letters stand for a technology that makes digital images and creatures, such as the dinosaurs of Jurassic Park and the Na'vi of Avatar. For 10 points, give this abbreviation for computer-generated imagery.

Released in 1927, this film starring Al Jolson is generally credited as the first feature-length movie with synchronized dialogue. It features songs and spoken lines, and it ended the era of silent films. For 10 points, name this film about a cantor's son who defies his father to perform popular music.

This silent film star was nicknamed "the Great Stone Face" because he almost never smiled. He did his own dangerous stunts in films such as The General and Sherlock Jr. For 10 points, name this American comedian.

In 1895, these two French brothers held a public screening of short films in a Paris cafe using their cinématographe. Auguste and Louis ran a photographic plate business in Lyon. For 10 points, name these early filmmakers whose surname means "light" in French.

This cartoon rabbit from Looney Tunes chews a carrot and asks "What's up, Doc?" He often outsmarts the hunter Elmer Fudd and the black duck Daffy, and he first appeared in the 1940 short A Wild Hare. For 10 points, name this Warner Bros. character.

In this 1950s sitcom, a redheaded woman gets into schemes while her husband Ricky Ricardo leads a band. Its title character was played by Lucille Ball. It was one of the first shows to be filmed before a live audience. For 10 points, name this show.
This puppeteer created Kermit the Frog and the other Muppets. He worked on Sesame Street and also directed The Dark Crystal. For 10 points, name this American creator of Fozzie Bear and Miss Piggy.

In film production, this person adds sounds like footsteps and breaking glass in a studio, matching them to actions on screen. For 10 points, give this job title, named for the sound-effects pioneer Jack.

This 1927 German silent science-fiction film directed by Fritz Lang is set in a city of towers where workers toil underground. It features a robot double of a woman named Maria. For 10 points, name this film.

text: This wrought-iron lattice tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair. It was designed by the firm of Gustave Eiffel, and many Parisians first protested it. It stands on the Champ de Mars. For 10 points, name this landmark of Paris.

This monument was built for the pharaoh Khufu on the west bank of the Nile. It was made from millions of limestone blocks and is the largest of the pyramids at its site. For 10 points, name this ancient Egyptian tomb near Cairo.

This elliptical amphitheater in Rome was built under the Flavian emperors and could seat tens of thousands. It hosted gladiator fights and had underground tunnels called the hypogeum. For 10 points, name this ruined arena.

This marble temple stands on the Acropolis in Athens and was dedicated to the goddess Athena. It was built in the fifth century BC in the Doric style and designed by Ictinus and Callicrates. For 10 points, name this ancient Greek temple.

This white marble mausoleum in Agra, India, was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. He built it for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It has four minarets and a large central dome. For 10 points, name this building.

This long fortification stretches across northern China. Built and rebuilt over many dynasties, it was meant to protect against nomadic invaders. Its Ming dynasty sections are best known. For 10 points, name this structure.

This American architect designed Fallingwater, a house built over a waterfall in Pennsylvania. He developed the Prairie School and designed the spiraling Guggenheim Museum in New York City. For 10 points, name this architect who founded Taliesin.

This style developed in medieval France and features pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and large stained-glass windows. Cathedrals built in it use flying buttresses to support high walls. For 10 points, name this architectural style of Chartres and Reims.

This building type has a steel frame that supports its weight, allowing great height. The invention of the safety elevator by Elisha Otis helped make it practical. Chicago and New York pioneered it. For 10 points, name this type of very tall building.

This opera house on Bennelong Point is topped with sail-like white shells. It was designed by the Danish architect Jørn Utzon and opened in 1973. For 10 points, name this landmark of an Australian harbor city.
This Catalan architect designed the Casa Batlló and Park Güell. His unfinished church, the Sagrada Família, is full of curves and nature-inspired forms. For 10 points, name this Barcelona architect.

This building at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue was designed by James Hoban and has been the home of presidents since John Adams. It was burned by the British in 1814. For 10 points, name this building in Washington, DC.

This sixth-century church in Constantinople was commissioned by Justinian and features a giant dome supported on pendentives. It was later turned into a mosque, with minarets added. For 10 points, name this Byzantine building in Istanbul.

This German-American architect said "Less is more" and designed the Seagram Building in New York City. His steel-and-glass buildings include Crown Hall and the Barcelona Pavilion. For 10 points, name this Bauhaus director.

This curved structure spans an opening and is held together at the top by a wedge-shaped stone called the keystone. The Romans used it widely in bridges and aqueducts. For 10 points, name this structure also seen at the McDonald's logo.

This Greek column style is topped with a capital decorated with acanthus leaves. Its columns are tall and slender. For 10 points, name this style, the most ornate of the three, which is the last in the sequence Doric, Ionic, and this one.

This tilting bell tower stands in the Piazza dei Miracoli in Tuscany. It began leaning during construction because it was built on soft soil. Legend says Galileo dropped balls from it. For 10 points, name this campanile.
Salisbury Plain in England is the location of this prehistoric monument of huge standing stones in a circle. It aligns with the sun at the summer solstice. For 10 points, name this site.

This Inca citadel stands high in the Andes above the Urubamba River in Peru. It was abandoned and unknown to the outside world until Hiram Bingham brought attention to it in 1911. For 10 points, name this site.

This Swiss-French architect wrote that a house is "a machine for living in." He designed the Villa Savoye and the Unité d'Habitation. For 10 points, name this Swiss-French architect who wrote Toward an Architecture.

This Roman building in Rome has a huge concrete dome with an opening at the top called the oculus. It was rebuilt under Hadrian and later became a church. For 10 points, name this temple to all the gods.

In Gothic cathedrals, these exterior arched supports carry the thrust of the roof to heavy piers outside the walls. They allowed walls to be thinner and filled with windows. For 10 points, name these supports at Notre-Dame.

This red suspension bridge connects San Francisco with Marin County. It was opened in 1937 and is painted a color called International Orange. For 10 points, name this bridge across a strait of the same name.

This Art Deco skyscraper on Fifth Avenue in New York City opened in 1931. It has 102 floors and features a tall mast that was meant for airships. King Kong climbed it in a film. For 10 points, name this building.

This 1920s and 1930s style features geometric zigzags, sunbursts, and stylized ornament. The Chrysler Building is a famous example. For 10 points, name this style whose name comes from a Paris exposition of decorative arts.

This palace outside Paris was built by Louis XIV and has a Hall of Mirrors. Its gardens were designed by André Le Nôtre. The Treaty ending World War I with Germany was signed in it. For 10 points, name this palace.

This Canadian-American architect used curving sheets of titanium on the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao. He also designed the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles. For 10 points, name this deconstructivist architect.

This Chinese-American architect designed a glass pyramid for the courtyard of the Louvre. He also designed the East Building of the National Gallery of Art and the John Hancock Tower in Boston. For 10 points, name this architect.

This medieval fortress-palace sits on a hill above Granada, Spain, and was the last stronghold of the Moors. It has a Court of the Lions with a fountain on twelve statues. For 10 points, name this Nasrid complex.

This Gothic cathedral stands on an island in the Seine in Paris. Its towers, rose windows, and flying buttresses inspired Victor Hugo's novel about a hunchback named Quasimodo. A fire damaged its roof and spire in 2019. For 10 points, name this cathedral whose name means "Our Lady."

text: This London playhouse was built in 1599 on the south bank of the Thames by the company of Richard Burbage. Many plays by its resident playwright premiered there, and it burned down in 1613. A modern reconstruction stands nearby. For 10 points, name this round, open-air Elizabethan theater.

In this art form, dancers wear tutus and special shoes that let them stand on the tips of their toes. It developed in Renaissance Italy and was refined in France and Russia. Swan Lake and Giselle are classic examples. For 10 points, name this dance form with positions such as plié and arabesque.

This American photographer made black-and-white pictures of Yosemite Valley and the American West. He cofounded Group f/64 and developed the Zone System for controlling exposure. For 10 points, name this photographer of Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico.

This photographer worked for the Farm Security Administration during the Great Depression. Her photograph of a worried mother with her children in a pea-picker's camp is called Migrant Mother. For 10 points, name this woman.

This street in New York City runs through the theater district near Times Square. Musicals such as The Phantom of the Opera and The Lion King have long runs on its stages. For 10 points, name this theater center, whose name also refers to professional stage productions in New York.

These annual awards for live theater on Broadway are named for the actress Antoinette Perry. Winners receive a medal and are named in categories such as Best Musical and Best Play. For 10 points, name these awards.

This 2015 hip-hop musical by Lin-Manuel Miranda tells the story of a Treasury secretary who was born in the Caribbean. It features songs like "My Shot" and "The Room Where It Happens." For 10 points, name this musical about the first Secretary of the Treasury.

This choreographer founded a company in New York in 1926 and created a modern dance technique based on contraction and release of the torso. Her works include Appalachian Spring, with music by Aaron Copland. For 10 points, name this pioneer of modern dance.

This American choreographer founded a dance theater in 1958 whose best-known work is Revelations, set to spirituals. His company is based in New York City. For 10 points, name this African-American dance pioneer.

This Japanese art involves folding a single square sheet of paper into shapes without cutting it. A popular model is the crane, and legend says folding a thousand grants a wish. For 10 points, name this art.

In this craft, artists shape wet clay into forms like bowls and vases, often on a spinning wheel. The pieces are then dried and fired in a kiln, and many are covered with a glaze. For 10 points, name this craft.

This performance art relies only on gesture and facial expression, with no spoken words. Marcel Marceau made it famous with his character Bip, and a classic trick is pretending to be trapped in a box. For 10 points, name this silent art.

This Russian director and teacher cofounded the Moscow Art Theatre. His acting system asked actors to draw on emotional memory and objectives, and it inspired American method acting. For 10 points, name this author of An Actor Prepares.

This Japanese form of musical drama features performers in carved wooden masks and very slow, stylized movements. Plays are often about ghosts and are written by playwrights like Zeami. For 10 points, name this classical theater tradition.

This French artist and inventor developed a photographic process in the 1830s that fixed an image on a silvered copper plate. A picture made with it is named after him. For 10 points, name this man who worked with Joseph Nicéphore Niépce.

In ballet, this word names a quick spin on one foot, with the other leg raised to the side or held against the knee. It is French for "whirl," and dancers called fouettés repeat a related turn in Swan Lake. For 10 points, name this dance move.

This Italian theater form from the sixteenth century used stock characters like Harlequin and Pantalone, improvised dialogue, and masks. It means "comedy of the profession." For 10 points, name this tradition that influenced Moliere.

This art of beautiful handwriting uses pens with broad nibs or brushes and has traditions in Arabic, Chinese, and European scripts. Illuminated manuscripts by monks are a famous example. For 10 points, name this art.

In this art form, pieces of paper, cloth, photographs, and other flat materials are glued to a surface to make a composition. Picasso and Braque pioneered it in painting. For 10 points, name this technique whose name comes from the French for "glue."

In this style of dance, dancers wear shoes with metal plates on the heel and toe to make rhythmic sounds. Fred Astaire and Gene Kelly used it in movies, and Bill Robinson was a famous practitioner. For 10 points, name this dance.

This ballroom dance has three beats to a measure and a smooth, turning step. It became popular in Vienna in the nineteenth century, with music by Johann Strauss. For 10 points, name this dance in three-four time.
This passionate dance and song style from Andalusia in Spain features guitar, hand clapping, and fast footwork. Dancers sometimes use fans and castanets. For 10 points, name this Spanish art.

This German design school was founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919. It combined crafts and fine arts and taught that form should follow function. It later moved to Dessau. For 10 points, name this school that influenced modern architecture and design.

This art form makes images from tiny pieces of colored stone, glass, or tile called tesserae. Byzantine churches in Ravenna are famous for it, and Roman villas often had floors decorated with it. For 10 points, name this art.

In theater, this term names the area of the stage farthest from the audience. Stages were once built on a slope so that this area was higher. For 10 points, name this direction, the opposite of downstage.

This craft joins pieces of fabric, often with a batting layer between, using stitching in patterns. Women from Gee's Bend, Alabama, are famous for their patterns, and the Amish also made them. For 10 points, name this craft.

This urban dance style began in the Bronx in the 1970s alongside hip-hop music. It includes spins on the back or head and moves such as the windmill and the freeze. For 10 points, name this dance, also called b-boying.

This traditional Japanese theater features all-male casts, stylized makeup called kumadori, and a walkway through the audience called hanamichi. Actors known as onnagata play female roles. For 10 points, name this theater.
This French photographer, a cofounder of Magnum Photos, wrote about the "decisive moment" in photography. He photographed Paris street scenes with a small Leica camera. For 10 points, name this man.

The Tlingit, Haida, and other peoples of the Pacific Northwest carve these tall wooden poles from cedar. They display figures like ravens and bears that represent family histories. For 10 points, name this type of carved monument.

text: This river's delta includes the Atchafalaya Basin and is rapidly losing wetlands. Its tributaries include the Arkansas and the Ohio. It begins at Lake Itasca in Minnesota. For 10 points, name this longest river system in the United States by many measures, which flows through New Orleans to the Gulf of Mexico.

This canyon was carved over millions of years by a river and is more than a mile deep in places. Its South Rim is reached from the town of Tusayan. The Hualapai and Havasupai peoples live near it. For 10 points, name this Arizona landmark carved by the Colorado River.

This mountain range runs from New Mexico through Colorado and Wyoming to Montana, forming the Continental Divide. Pikes Peak and Longs Peak are in its Colorado section. Denver sits just east of it. For 10 points, name this North American mountain range.

This state was purchased from Russia in 1867 for about seven million dollars. Its capital is Juneau and its largest city is Anchorage. It is the largest state by area. For 10 points, name this northwesternmost state of the United States.
This state is made up of volcanic islands in the Pacific, including Maui, Kauai, and Oahu. Its capital is Honolulu. Pearl Harbor is on one of its islands. For 10 points, name this fiftieth state.

This lake is the largest of the Great Lakes by surface area. Its southern shore includes the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, and Duluth is a port on its western tip. The Edmund Fitzgerald sank in it in 1975. For 10 points, name this Great Lake.

This mountain range stretches from Georgia and Alabama north to Maine and Canada. The Blue Ridge and the Great Smoky Mountains are parts of it. A famous long hiking trail follows its crest. For 10 points, name this eastern mountain system.

This national park straddles the California and Nevada border and contains Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America. It is known for extreme summer heat. For 10 points, name this desert valley in the Mojave region.

This state is a peninsula with Miami on its southeast coast and Tallahassee as its capital. Walt Disney World and Cape Canaveral are located there. Its southern tip includes the Keys. For 10 points, name this southeastern "Sunshine State."
This state's capital is Austin, and its largest cities include Houston and Dallas. It borders Mexico along the Rio Grande. The Alamo is in San Antonio. For 10 points, name this "Lone Star State."
This lake in Utah is saltier than the ocean, so swimmers float easily. It is the remnant of the ancient Lake Bonneville. Antelope Island sits in it. For 10 points, name this lake near Salt Lake City.

This monument in the Black Hills of South Dakota features carved faces of four presidents. Gutzon Borglum directed its sculpting. The presidents shown include Washington and Lincoln. For 10 points, name this mountain monument.

This national park in Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho is home to the geyser Old Faithful. It was established in 1872 as the first national park in the United States. Bison and grizzly bears live there. For 10 points, name this park.

These waterfalls on the border of New York and Ontario include the American Falls and the Horseshoe Falls. The Maid of the Mist boat carries visitors close to them. The Niagara River flows over them. For 10 points, name these waterfalls.
This city on Lake Michigan is nicknamed the "Windy City." It is home to Wrigley Field and the Willis Tower. Its river was famously reversed in 1900. For 10 points, name this largest city in Illinois.

This river rises in Montana and flows southeast to join the Mississippi River near Saint Louis. Lewis and Clark traveled up it. It is nicknamed the "Big Muddy." For 10 points, name this longest river in the United States by length of its main stem.

This river carved the Grand Canyon and is dammed at Lake Mead and Lake Powell. It begins in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado. Its water is divided among several western states and Mexico. For 10 points, name this river that flows into the Gulf of California.
The highest mountain in North America, formerly named for a president, is found in this state. It lies in the Alaska Range. For 10 points, name this mountain, whose Native name means "the high one."

This flat grassland region of the central United States stretches from Texas to the Dakotas, east of the Rocky Mountains. Bison once roamed it in huge herds. The 1930s Dust Bowl struck it. For 10 points, name this region of prairie.

This Louisiana city sits near the mouth of the Mississippi River and is famed for jazz and Mardi Gras. Hurricane Katrina flooded it in 2005. Its French Quarter is a major attraction. For 10 points, name this city.

The capital of the United States is located in this district, which is not part of any state. It lies on the Potomac River between Maryland and Virginia. For 10 points, give the name of this district that includes the White House and the Capitol.

This is the only Great Lake located entirely within the United States. Chicago and Milwaukee lie on its shores. It is connected to Lake Huron by the Straits of Mackinac. For 10 points, name this lake.

This desert in southern California and Nevada contains Joshua trees and a national preserve. It lies between Los Angeles and Las Vegas. Barstow is in it. For 10 points, name this North American desert.

This state has the largest population in the United States. Sacramento is its capital, and it has the cities of Los Angeles and San Francisco. Its coast is on the Pacific Ocean. For 10 points, name this "Golden State."
This large wetland of sawgrass and mangroves is located in southern Florida. It is a national park home to alligators, manatees, and the Florida panther. For 10 points, name this "River of Grass."

This river forms the southern border of Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois. It joins the Mississippi River at Cairo, Illinois. Cincinnati and Pittsburgh are along it or its headwaters. For 10 points, name this river.

This inlet of the Pacific Ocean in Washington State includes Seattle and Tacoma on its shores. It was named for a lieutenant on George Vancouver's expedition. Ferries cross it to islands like Bainbridge. For 10 points, name this sound in the Pacific Northwest.

This dam on the Colorado River, on the Nevada-Arizona border, was completed in 1936. It created Lake Mead. It was built during the Great Depression. For 10 points, name this famous dam near Las Vegas.

This red suspension bridge connects San Francisco to Marin County. It opened in 1937 across a strait that leads to the Pacific Ocean. Fog often covers its towers. For 10 points, name this California bridge.

This peninsula in Massachusetts has a hooked shape and includes Provincetown at its tip. The Pilgrims first landed near its end in 1620. Its towns include Hyannis and Chatham. For 10 points, name this vacation destination on the Atlantic coast.

text: This river flows north through Uganda, Sudan, and Egypt and empties into the Mediterranean Sea through a large delta. The Blue Nile and White Nile join at Khartoum. The Aswan High Dam is on it. For 10 points, name this river of ancient Egypt.

This river in South America carries more water than any other river and flows through Brazil and Peru. Manaus lies on it. Its basin holds the largest tropical rainforest. For 10 points, name this river.

This is the largest hot desert in the world, covering much of northern Africa. Camels carry travelers across its dunes. It stretches from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea. For 10 points, name this desert.

Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first climbed this mountain in 1953. It lies on the border of Nepal and China. It is the highest mountain above sea level. For 10 points, name this peak in the Himalayas.
This country is both a continent and a nation. Its capital is Canberra, and its largest city is Sydney. Kangaroos and koalas live there. For 10 points, name this country in the Southern Hemisphere.
This island country in East Asia is made up of four main islands, including Honshu and Hokkaido. Its capital is Tokyo. Mount Fuji is its highest peak. For 10 points, name this country.

This country is the largest in South America and the only one where Portuguese is the main language. Its capital is Brasilia. Rio de Janeiro is its famous coastal city. For 10 points, name this country.
This country in northeastern Africa is home to the pyramids at Giza and the city of Cairo. The Suez Canal crosses it. Its ancient pharaohs ruled along the Nile. For 10 points, name this country.
This South Asian country has New Delhi as its capital and the Ganges as a sacred river. Its cities include Mumbai and Kolkata. The Taj Mahal is in Agra. For 10 points, name this country.

This mountain range separates the Indian subcontinent from the Tibetan Plateau. It includes Kangchenjunga. Nepal and Bhutan lie within it. For 10 points, name this range, home to the world's highest peaks.

This is the largest and deepest ocean, covering about a third of the Earth's surface. It contains the Mariana Trench and the Ring of Fire. It borders Asia and the Americas. For 10 points, name this ocean.

This continent around the South Pole is covered by a thick ice sheet and has no permanent residents. Penguins live on its coasts. Scientists staff research stations there. For 10 points, name this southernmost continent.

This country is the second largest in the world by area and has Ottawa as its capital. It has ten provinces and three territories. Toronto and Vancouver are its large cities. For 10 points, name this country north of the United States.
This country to the south of the United States has a capital built on the ruins of Tenochtitlan. Its language is Spanish. The Yucatan Peninsula is in it. For 10 points, name this country.

This country spans eleven time zones and is the largest in the world by area. Its cities include Saint Petersburg and Vladivostok. Moscow is its capital. The Trans-Siberian Railway crosses it. For 10 points, name this country.
This country's shape resembles a boot, and its capital is Rome. It contains the cities of Venice and Florence. Mount Vesuvius is near Naples. For 10 points, name this country in southern Europe.

This mountain range runs along the western edge of South America and is the longest continental mountain range. Machu Picchu was built in it. Aconcagua is its highest peak. For 10 points, name this range.
This coral system lies off the northeast coast of Queensland, Australia. It is made up of thousands of individual reefs. It can be seen from space. For 10 points, name this largest coral reef system.

This imaginary line circles the Earth at zero degrees latitude, dividing the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Ecuador is named for it. It passes through Kenya and Indonesia. For 10 points, name this line.

This is the largest island in the world that is not a continent. It is an autonomous territory of Denmark, and most of it is covered by ice. Nuuk is its capital. For 10 points, name this island northeast of Canada.

This island nation off the southeast coast of Africa is home to lemurs. Its capital is Antananarivo. It is the fourth largest island in the world. For 10 points, name this country in the Indian Ocean.

This waterway cuts across a narrow isthmus and links the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. It uses locks and opened in 1914. Ships pass through Gatun Lake. For 10 points, name this canal in Central America.

This sea is bordered by Spain, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt, and Morocco. It connects to the Atlantic through the Strait of Gibraltar. Crete and Sicily are islands in it. For 10 points, name this sea.
This European mountain range includes Mont Blanc and the Matterhorn. It stretches across Switzerland, France, Italy, and Austria. Hannibal crossed it with elephants. For 10 points, name this range.

This capital of Egypt sits on the Nile near its delta. The Giza Pyramids are just outside it. Its Tahrir Square is famous, and its old district has the Khan el-Khalili bazaar. For 10 points, name this city.

This capital of Japan was once called Edo. The Imperial Palace is in it. The Shibuya crossing and the Sumida River are located there, and the Olympics were held there in 1964. For 10 points, name this city.

This city straddles Europe and Asia across the Bosphorus. It was once called Constantinople. The Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque stand there. A bridge across the strait connects its European and Asian sides. For 10 points, name this largest city in Turkey.
This landlocked country in the Alps is known for its neutrality and chocolate. Its cities include Zurich, Geneva, and Bern. Its flag is a white cross on red. For 10 points, name this country.

This mountain in Tanzania is the highest in Africa. It is a dormant volcano with snow near its top, and it has three volcanic cones named Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira. Hikers climb it from towns like Moshi. For 10 points, name this peak.
This river is the longest in Asia and flows from the Tibetan Plateau through Chongqing and Wuhan to Shanghai. The Three Gorges Dam is on it. For 10 points, name this Chinese river.
This desert in Mongolia and northern China is cold and rocky. Genghis Khan's empire arose nearby, and dinosaur fossils have been found there. For 10 points, name this Asian desert.

text: Alexander Graham Bell is usually credited with patenting this device in 1876. His assistant Thomas Watson heard the first words spoken over it. It converts sound into electrical signals and back into sound. For 10 points, name this communication device that has a handset and a dial or keypad.

Thomas Edison developed a long-lasting version of this device in 1879 using a carbon filament. It glows when electric current heats a thin wire. Joseph Swan independently developed a similar one in England. For 10 points, name this lighting device that is screwed into a lamp.

Orville and Wilbur made the first sustained, powered flights of this type of vehicle at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903. Their first one was called the Flyer. It has wings and an engine or propeller. For 10 points, name this vehicle invented by the Wright brothers.

Johannes Gutenberg developed this machine in Germany around 1440, using movable metal type. His most famous product was a Bible with forty-two lines per page. It greatly increased the spread of books in Europe. For 10 points, name this invention.

Families gather on the fourth Thursday of November for this American holiday, which features turkey and pumpkin pie. It commemorates a harvest feast shared by the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag. Abraham Lincoln proclaimed it a national holiday during the Civil War. For 10 points, name this holiday.

On this holiday, which falls on October 31, children wear costumes and go trick-or-treating. Jack-o'-lanterns carved from pumpkins are common decorations. It grew from the Celtic festival of Samhain. For 10 points, name this autumn holiday.

Every four years, an extra day is added to February in this kind of year to keep the calendar aligned with the Earth's orbit. The year 2000 was one, but 1900 was not. People born on February 29 celebrate birthdays only in this kind of year. For 10 points, name this type of year with 366 days.

This statue on an island in New York Harbor was a gift from France in 1886. Frederic Bartholdi designed it, and Gustave Eiffel built its iron framework. It holds a torch and a tablet. For 10 points, name this symbol of liberty.

This sporting event was revived in 1896 in Athens by Pierre de Coubertin. Its symbol is five interlocking rings of different colors. It takes place every four years in summer and winter versions. For 10 points, name this international athletic competition that began in ancient Greece.

A Frenchman who lost his sight as a child developed this writing system in the 1820s. It uses patterns of raised dots arranged in cells. Readers feel the dots with their fingertips. For 10 points, name this reading system for people who are blind.

Samuel Morse helped develop this system for sending messages over telegraph wires. It uses combinations of short and long signals called dots and dashes. The distress signal SOS is famous in it. For 10 points, name this code.
This tower in Paris was built for the 1889 World's Fair. It is made of wrought iron and named for its engineer. It stands on the Champ de Mars. For 10 points, name this French landmark.

This long defensive structure in northern China was built and rebuilt by many dynasties, notably the Ming. Watchtowers dot its length. It stretches across mountains and deserts. For 10 points, name this wall.

This British passenger liner sank in the North Atlantic in April 1912 after striking an iceberg. It was said to be unsinkable on its maiden voyage from Southampton. More than 1,500 people died. For 10 points, name this ship.

This black stone slab, found in Egypt in 1799, was inscribed with the same decree in three scripts. Jean-Francois Champollion used it to decipher hieroglyphs. It is now kept in the British Museum. For 10 points, name this key to Egyptian writing.

Players of this board game for two move sixteen pieces each across sixty-four squares. Its pieces include the knight, bishop, and rook. The goal is to trap the opposing king. For 10 points, name this game, whose winning condition is called checkmate.

The Great Seal of the United States and many coins display this bird of prey. It has a white head and tail as an adult, and it appears on the Great Seal adopted in 1782. It eats fish. For 10 points, name this bird, the national emblem.

This bell in Philadelphia has a famous crack and bears the inscription "Proclaim Liberty throughout all the land." It was housed in Independence Hall. It became a symbol of American independence and abolition. For 10 points, name this bell.

Riders on this mail service, started in 1860, carried letters between Missouri and California on horseback. Riders changed horses at relay stations. It ended after the telegraph connected the coasts. For 10 points, name this short-lived western mail service.

This white marble mausoleum in Agra was built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It has a large dome and four minarets. It sits beside the Yamuna River. For 10 points, name this Indian landmark.

This large ancient arena in Rome hosted gladiator fights. Construction was finished under the emperor Titus in 80 CE. Its official name was the Flavian Amphitheater. For 10 points, name this oval stadium in Rome.

This Incan citadel sits high in the Andes above the Urubamba River in Peru. Hiram Bingham brought it to world attention in 1911. Its terraced stone buildings were built in the fifteenth century. For 10 points, name this ruin near Cusco.

This prehistoric ring of standing stones stands on Salisbury Plain in England. Its largest stones are arranged in a circle with horizontal lintels. Some blue stones were moved from Wales. For 10 points, name this monument.

This magnetic instrument has a needle that always points north. Sailors used it for navigation beginning in medieval times. It was invented in China. For 10 points, name this tool that helps travelers find direction.

This Polish-born scientist was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. She discovered polonium and radium with her husband Pierre. For 10 points, name this woman who won in both physics and chemistry.

This German-born physicist developed the theory of relativity and the equation E equals m c squared. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921 for the photoelectric effect. He moved to Princeton in 1933. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This woman lost her sight and hearing as an infant but graduated from Radcliffe College. Her teacher Anne Sullivan spelled words into her hand. She wrote The Story of My Life. For 10 points, name this American author and activist.

This painter, sculptor, and inventor drew the Vitruvian Man and sketched flying machines. He painted The Last Supper and was born in the town of Vinci. His notebooks are written in mirror writing. For 10 points, name this Italian Renaissance polymath.

This American astronaut was the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969, as commander of Apollo 11. His words included "one small step for man." He was joined by Buzz Aldrin. For 10 points, name this astronaut.

This woman was the first female pilot to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean, in 1932. She disappeared over the Pacific in 1937 during an attempt to fly around the world. Her navigator was Fred Noonan. For 10 points, name this aviator.

This American statesman is pictured on the hundred-dollar bill. He flew a kite in a thunderstorm, invented bifocals and the lightning rod, and published Poor Richard's Almanack. For 10 points, name this founding father.

text: This is the base unit of length in the metric system. It is slightly longer than a yard, and one hundred centimeters make one of these. Track events like the one hundred dash are measured in it. For 10 points, name this unit of length.
This is the base unit of mass in the metric system. It is divided into one thousand grams. It was once defined by a platinum-iridium cylinder kept near Paris. For 10 points, name this unit of mass.

On this temperature scale, water freezes at zero degrees and boils at one hundred degrees at sea level. It is named for a Swedish astronomer. Most of the world uses it for weather reports. For 10 points, name this scale.
This word describes a group of twelve items. Eggs are often sold in this quantity in a carton. Half of it is six, and a baker's one is sometimes thirteen. For 10 points, name this unit.
This word describes a period of ten years. The 1990s and the 1920s are examples. It comes from the Greek word for ten, and it is shorter than a generation. For 10 points, name this unit of time.

This word describes a period of one hundred years. The twentieth one began in 1901 by strict counting. It comes from a Latin word for one hundred, and its adjective is also the name of a plant. For 10 points, name this unit of time.

This system of numerals uses letters such as I, V, X, L, C, D, and M. The letter L stands for fifty in it. It was used in ancient Rome. For 10 points, name this numbering system still seen on clock faces and movie credits.

Melvil Dewey developed this library classification system in 1876. It assigns numbers from 000 to 999 to broad subject areas. Books are shelved by these numbers. For 10 points, name this system used in many school libraries.

Noah Webster published a famous American example of this type of book in 1828. It lists words alphabetically with their meanings, spellings, and pronunciations. The Oxford English one is another well-known example. For 10 points, name this reference work.

L. L. Zamenhof created this constructed language in 1887 as a neutral means of communication between nations. Its name means "one who hopes." It has regular grammar with no irregular verbs. For 10 points, name this artificial language.
This ancient language of Rome gave English many roots, such as aqua and terra. It is the source of the Romance languages. Julius Caesar wrote in it. For 10 points, name this language.

The first letter of this alphabet is alpha and the last is omega. Its letters are used in math and science and fraternity names. It was adapted from the Phoenician script. For 10 points, name this alphabet used in ancient Athens.

This alphabet is used in Russian and Bulgarian and was named for a missionary saint. It includes letters like Ж and Я. It was developed from Greek in the ninth century. For 10 points, name this writing system.

This word names a word with the same meaning as another, such as "big" and "large." The word is formed from Greek parts meaning "together" and "name." A thesaurus lists many of them. For 10 points, name this type of word.

This word names a word that means the opposite of another, such as "hot" and "cold." Its prefix comes from a Greek word meaning "against." A thesaurus often lists these along with synonyms. For 10 points, name this type of word.

This word names a word that reads the same forward and backward. Examples include "level," "radar," and "kayak." Some sentences, such as "Madam, I'm Adam," also have this property. For 10 points, name this kind of word.

This literary term describes a word that imitates a sound, such as "buzz," "splash," or "meow." Its name comes from Greek roots meaning "name making." Comic books use them in bold letters. For 10 points, name this figure of speech.

This is the study of the sounds, lengths, and stresses of speech. Linguists use a special alphabet to write them. Teachers of reading use it to explain how letters map to sounds. For 10 points, name the study of speech sounds.

This document of 1776, written chiefly by Thomas Jefferson, announced the thirteen colonies' separation from Britain. It begins "When in the Course of human events." For 10 points, name this document adopted on July 4.

King John of England was forced to seal this charter in 1215 at Runnymede. It limited royal power and promised the right to a lawful trial. Its name is Latin for "great charter." For 10 points, name this document.

The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution make up this document. It protects freedoms of speech, religion, and the press. James Madison drafted it. For 10 points, name this set of amendments.

Abraham Lincoln delivered this very short speech at a Pennsylvania battlefield in November 1863. It begins "Four score and seven years ago." It ends with a "government of the people, by the people, for the people." For 10 points, name this speech.

People in many countries use this system of units, based on tens, that includes the liter, meter, and gram. It was developed in France during the Revolution. The United States uses a different customary system. For 10 points, name this system.

On this temperature scale, water freezes at thirty-two degrees and boils at two hundred twelve degrees at sea level. It is named for a German physicist who also invented the mercury thermometer. The United States uses it for weather reports. For 10 points, name this scale.

This kind of triangle has three sides of equal length and three angles of sixty degrees. Its name comes from Latin roots meaning "equal sides." Every equiangular triangle is also one of these. For 10 points, name this triangle.

This instrument measures atmospheric pressure and was invented by Evangelista Torricelli. Its name comes from Greek words for "weight" and "measure." Falling readings often predict a storm. For 10 points, name this weather instrument.
This device with a gnomon casts a shadow to tell time. Ancient Egyptians and Greeks used it. It cannot work at night or on cloudy days. For 10 points, name this timekeeping device.

This tool with a flat scale of inches or centimeters is used to measure and draw straight lines. Students keep one in a pencil case. Wooden, plastic, and metal ones are common, and a longer version is a yardstick. For 10 points, name this tool.

This instrument with a needle and a circular scale of degrees measures the angle of a line or arc. Students use it in geometry class. It is usually semicircular and made of clear plastic. For 10 points, name this tool.

This English word names a book of maps. Its name comes from a Titan of Greek myth who held up the sky. Gerardus Mercator popularized the name in the sixteenth century. For 10 points, name this reference book.

text: In December 1773, colonists disguised as Mohawk Indians boarded three ships in a Massachusetts harbor. They dumped 342 chests of a taxed product overboard to protest the Tea Act. Parliament answered with the Coercive Acts, which the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. For 10 points, name this protest that took place in Boston.

This man was the principal author of a 1776 document that begins by asserting that all men are created equal. He later served as the third president of the United States. He lived at a Virginia estate called Monticello. For 10 points, name this author of the Declaration of Independence.

In 1803, Robert Livingston and James Monroe negotiated this deal with France. Napoleon sold roughly 828,000 square miles of land to the United States for 15 million dollars. It doubled the size of the young country and gave it control of the port of New Orleans. For 10 points, name this land purchase named for a territory west of the Mississippi River.

A young Shoshone woman named Sacagawea served as interpreter and guide on this journey. Thomas Jefferson ordered it to explore the lands west of the Mississippi River and find a water route to the Pacific. It was led by two men who set out from near Saint Louis in 1804. For 10 points, name this expedition led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark.

This speech begins with the words "Four score and seven years ago." It was delivered in November 1863 at the dedication of a cemetery for soldiers who died in a Pennsylvania battle. It ends by calling for a "new birth of freedom." For 10 points, name this short speech by Abraham Lincoln.

This woman escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and then returned to the South about thirteen times to guide others to freedom. She worked as a conductor on a network of safe houses and secret routes. She was nicknamed "Moses" by those she helped. For 10 points, name this abolitionist and conductor on the Underground Railroad.

Issued on January 1, 1863, this order declared that slaves in states in rebellion against the Union were free. It did not apply to the border states that stayed loyal to the Union. It changed the aims of the Civil War by making the end of slavery a goal of the Union. For 10 points, name this proclamation of Abraham Lincoln.

The Central Pacific and Union Pacific companies built this project from opposite directions. Chinese and Irish immigrants did much of the backbreaking labor. Its two lines were joined by a ceremonial golden spike at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869. For 10 points, name this rail line that connected the eastern and western halves of the United States.

On the morning of December 7, 1941, Japanese planes bombed American warships in Hawaii. Eight battleships were damaged or sunk, and more than 2,400 Americans were killed. The next day, Franklin Roosevelt called the date "a day that will live in infamy." For 10 points, name this attack that brought the United States into World War II.

In December 1955, this seamstress refused to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery, Alabama. Her arrest led to a boycott that lasted more than a year and made a young minister into a leader. She is often called the "mother of the civil rights movement." For 10 points, name this woman.

This man led the 1963 March on Washington, where he gave his "I Have a Dream" speech on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. He earned the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 for his use of nonviolent protest. He was assassinated in Memphis in 1968. For 10 points, name this Baptist minister and civil rights leader.

This president led the country through the Great Depression and most of World War II. He was elected four times and used radio "fireside chats" to speak directly to the public. His New Deal created programs such as Social Security and the Civilian Conservation Corps. For 10 points, name this president who served from 1933 to 1945.

This economic crisis began after the stock market crash of October 1929. Banks failed, factories closed, and about a quarter of American workers lost their jobs at its worst point. Soup kitchens and shantytowns known as Hoovervilles appeared in many cities. For 10 points, name this decade-long downturn that preceded the New Deal.

In the 1830s, the Cherokee and other southeastern tribes were forced to move to land west of the Mississippi River. Andrew Jackson had signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830. Thousands of Cherokee died of disease, cold, and hunger on the march to present-day Oklahoma. For 10 points, name this forced relocation whose name refers to weeping.

In 1848, James Marshall found shiny flakes in the American River at Sutter's Mill. News of the discovery drew about 300,000 people to California, many of them called forty-niners. San Francisco grew from a small village into a large city. For 10 points, name this rush that began in 1848.

In 1620, a group of English Separatists crossed the Atlantic on this ship and landed at Plymouth, Massachusetts. Before going ashore, 41 men signed a compact to govern themselves. For 10 points, name this ship that carried the Pilgrims to America.

The Virginia Company of London founded this colony in 1607 on a river named for the king. John Smith helped it survive a "starving time" by enforcing the rule that men who did not work did not eat. John Rolfe's tobacco later made the colony profitable. For 10 points, name this first permanent English settlement in North America.

James Madison proposed these amendments in 1789 to win over critics who feared a strong national government. Ratified in 1791, they protect freedoms of speech, religion, and the press. They also guarantee the right to a jury trial. For 10 points, name these first ten amendments to the Constitution.

This Philadelphia printer published Poor Richard's Almanack. He conducted a famous experiment with a kite and a key during a storm and invented bifocals. He also helped draft the Declaration of Independence and appears on the hundred-dollar bill. For 10 points, name this American statesman and inventor.

This man was the first Secretary of the Treasury under George Washington. He wrote most of the Federalist Papers with James Madison and John Jay and created the First Bank of the United States. He died in a duel with Aaron Burr in 1804. For 10 points, name this man who appears on the ten-dollar bill.

Completed in 1825 under Governor DeWitt Clinton, this man-made waterway linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie. It lowered shipping costs and helped turn New York City into the nation's leading port. Critics had mocked it as "Clinton's Ditch." For 10 points, name this canal in New York State.

In 1793, this inventor patented a machine that quickly separated seeds from short-staple cotton. It made cotton farming far more profitable and increased the demand for enslaved labor in the South. He also promoted the idea of interchangeable parts for muskets. For 10 points, name this American inventor of the cotton gin.

In December 1903, two brothers from Dayton, Ohio, made the first powered, controlled airplane flights near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The longest of their first four flights that day lasted 59 seconds. Their plane was named the Flyer. For 10 points, name these two brothers, Orville and Wilbur.

Born into slavery in Maryland, this man taught himself to read and escaped to the North in 1838. He published an autobiography called Narrative of the Life and wrote for his newspaper The North Star. He later advised Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this great abolitionist orator.

Beginning in the early 1930s, drought and poor farming practices turned the Great Plains into this disaster zone. Huge dust storms swept across Oklahoma, Kansas, and Texas and forced many families to flee to California. John Steinbeck described this migration in The Grapes of Wrath. For 10 points, name this environmental disaster of the 1930s.

In October 1962, American spy planes photographed Soviet missile sites under construction on an island in the Caribbean. President John F. Kennedy ordered a naval blockade, which he called a quarantine. After tense days, Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. For 10 points, name this Cold War confrontation over Cuba.

This president led the Rough Riders up San Juan Hill in the Spanish-American War. As president, he broke up trusts, created national parks, and began building the Panama Canal. His motto was to "speak softly and carry a big stick." For 10 points, name this man who served from 1901 to 1909.

In October 1781, General Charles Cornwallis surrendered his army to George Washington at this Virginia town. French ships blocked the British escape by sea while French and American soldiers surrounded the town on land. The surrender effectively ended major fighting in the American Revolution. For 10 points, name this battle.

Passed in 1820, this law admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state. It also banned slavery in the Louisiana Territory north of the 36 degrees 30 minutes line. Henry Clay helped broker it to preserve the balance in the Senate. For 10 points, name this agreement.

Issued in 1823, this policy was announced in a message to Congress by a president from Virginia. It warned European powers not to colonize or interfere in the Western Hemisphere. In return, the United States promised to stay out of European affairs. For 10 points, name this foreign policy statement named for James Monroe.

In 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the opinion in this case, which arose when William Marbury did not receive his commission as a justice of the peace. The Court ruled that part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional. This established the power of judicial review. For 10 points, name this case.

In 1857, the Supreme Court ruled in this case that African Americans could not be citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. Chief Justice Roger Taney wrote the opinion. It outraged northerners and helped push the nation toward civil war. For 10 points, name this case brought by an enslaved man from Missouri.
