text: In June 1215, English barons forced King John to put his seal on this document at Runnymede. It said that the king was subject to the law and promised that free men could not be punished except by lawful judgment. Its name is Latin for "Great Charter." For 10 points, name this document that limited royal power in England.

This English king broke with the Roman Catholic Church in the 1530s so that he could end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. Parliament made him head of the Church of England through the Act of Supremacy. He married six times, including Anne Boleyn and Jane Seymour. For 10 points, name this Tudor king.

This daughter of Anne Boleyn became queen in 1558 and ruled for 44 years. Her reign saw the defeat of a Spanish fleet and the plays of William Shakespeare. She never married and was called the Virgin Queen. For 10 points, name this Tudor monarch.

This Corsican-born general crowned himself emperor of the French in 1804 in Notre-Dame Cathedral. He won victories across Europe and then lost most of his army in a disastrous winter retreat from Moscow. His legal reforms are known as the Civil Code. For 10 points, name this French ruler.

In July 1789, a Paris crowd stormed this fortress and prison, which symbolized royal tyranny. Its fall is celebrated in France every July 14. The event is usually seen as the start of the French Revolution. For 10 points, name this fortress.

This king of France ruled for 72 years, from 1643 to 1715. He called himself the Sun King and built an enormous palace outside Paris that became the center of his court. He fought several expensive wars to expand French power. For 10 points, name this monarch.

This disease reached Europe in 1347 on trading ships from the Black Sea. Carried by fleas on rats, it killed a huge share of the continent's population over the next few years. Its victims developed painful swellings called buboes. For 10 points, name this medieval plague.

This "rebirth" of art and learning began in the Italian city-states in the 1300s. Wealthy patrons such as the Medici family paid artists to create new works. Thinkers called humanists studied the writings of ancient Greece and Rome. For 10 points, name this period of European history that produced Michelangelo and Raphael.

This painter and inventor filled thousands of pages of notebooks with drawings of flying machines and human anatomy. He painted The Last Supper in Milan and a portrait of a woman with a famous smile. He was born in the town of Vinci. For 10 points, name this Italian Renaissance genius who painted the Mona Lisa.

In 1517, a German monk is said to have nailed his Ninety-five Theses to the door of a church in Wittenberg. He attacked the sale of indulgences and taught that people are saved by faith alone. His ideas began the Protestant Reformation. For 10 points, name this German reformer.

Around 1450, a German goldsmith from Mainz developed a way to print with movable metal type. His most famous product was a Latin Bible. The invention made books cheaper and helped spread ideas across Europe. For 10 points, name this man, the inventor of the European printing press.

In 1588, King Philip II of Spain sent about 130 ships under the Duke of Medina Sidonia to invade England. English fire ships scattered the fleet at Calais, and storms wrecked many of the survivors on the way home. The defeat was a triumph for Elizabeth I. For 10 points, name this failed invasion fleet.

On June 18, 1815, a French army was defeated in a battle in present-day Belgium. The Duke of Wellington held the line until Prussian troops under Gebhard von Blucher arrived. Napoleon was exiled again after this loss. For 10 points, name this battle.

This revolution began in Great Britain in the late 1700s. Inventions such as the spinning jenny and James Watt's improved steam engine moved production from homes to factories. Cities grew rapidly as workers left farms. For 10 points, name this shift to machine-based manufacturing.

This war began in 1914 after the assassination of an Austrian archduke. The Allied Powers, including France, Britain, and Russia, fought the Central Powers, including Germany and Austria-Hungary. Fighting along the Western Front bogged down in trenches. For 10 points, name this conflict that ended in 1918.

On June 28, 1914, this nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb fired the shots that killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo. He belonged to a group seeking to unite Slavic peoples. Because of his age, he was spared the death penalty and died in prison in 1918. For 10 points, name this assassin whose act set off World War I.

Signed in 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors, this treaty ended World War I with Germany. It required Germany to give up land, limit its army, and accept responsibility for the war. Many Germans bitterly resented its terms. For 10 points, name this treaty named for a French palace.

This man became chancellor of Germany in 1933 and ruled as dictator until 1945. He wrote Mein Kampf while in prison and led the Nazi Party. His invasion of Poland in 1939 started World War II in Europe. For 10 points, name this German leader.

This man became British prime minister in May 1940 and promised the nation "blood, toil, tears and sweat." He led Britain through World War II and gave the "Iron Curtain" speech in 1946. He was also a painter and a Nobel Prize winner in Literature. For 10 points, name this British leader.

In the summer of 1940, the German Luftwaffe tried to win control of the skies over southern England. Radar and the skill of Spitfire and Hurricane pilots helped the Royal Air Force win. Hitler postponed his invasion plans. For 10 points, name this air campaign.

This event was the Nazi regime's systematic murder of about six million Jews and millions of other victims during World War II. Camps such as Auschwitz and Treblinka were built for this purpose. For 10 points, name this genocide.

Sailing in longships, these Scandinavian raiders attacked the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793. They later settled in Iceland, Normandy, and parts of England. Leif Erikson reached North America around the year 1000. For 10 points, name these seafaring people from Norway, Sweden, and Denmark.

This king of the Franks was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day in the year 800. He ruled much of western Europe and supported scholars at his court in Aachen. His name means "Charles the Great." For 10 points, name this ruler.

In 1066, Duke William of Normandy defeated King Harold Godwinson at this battle on the southeast coast of England. Harold was said to have been killed by an arrow. The Bayeux Tapestry shows scenes from this battle. For 10 points, name this battle that began the Norman conquest of England.

Beginning in 1095, European knights marched to the Middle East after Pope Urban II called for help against Muslim rulers. Their goal was to capture Jerusalem. Later expeditions included the Third, led in part by Richard the Lionheart. For 10 points, name these medieval religious wars.

This French peasant girl said that she heard the voices of saints telling her to drive out the English. She helped lift the siege of Orleans in 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned. She was burned at the stake in Rouen in 1431. For 10 points, name this saint and national heroine of France.

This Russian tsar traveled incognito in western Europe and returned to modernize his country. He founded the city of Saint Petersburg in 1703 and forced nobles to cut their beards. He defeated Sweden in the Great Northern War. For 10 points, name this ruler who ruled from 1682 to 1725.

This German-born empress seized power from her husband in 1762 and ruled Russia for over three decades. She corresponded with Voltaire and expanded Russian territory south to the Black Sea. For 10 points, name this woman, whose title includes the word "Great."

This Bolshevik leader returned to Russia in April 1917 and took power in the October Revolution. He founded the Soviet state and led it through a civil war. His body is on display in a mausoleum in Red Square. For 10 points, name this first leader of the Soviet Union.

As Minister President of Prussia, this man used wars against Denmark, Austria, and France to unify Germany in 1871. He was known as the "Iron Chancellor" and was said to favor "blood and iron." He later created the first social insurance programs. For 10 points, name this German statesman.

This lawyer led the Committee of Public Safety during the French Revolution. He oversaw the Reign of Terror, during which thousands were sent to the guillotine. He was himself guillotined in July 1794. For 10 points, name this Jacobin leader.

In October 1805, a British fleet under Horatio Nelson defeated the combined French and Spanish navies off the coast of Spain. Nelson was shot by a sniper and died during the battle. The victory ended Napoleon's hope of invading Britain. For 10 points, name this naval battle.

These treaties of 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War in the Holy Roman Empire. They recognized the independence of the Dutch Republic and the Swiss Confederation. They are often seen as the start of the modern system of sovereign states. For 10 points, name this peace.

After the defeat of Napoleon, diplomats met in this city from 1814 to 1815 to redraw Europe's map. Klemens von Metternich of Austria was its dominant figure. They sought a balance of power and restored many old ruling families. For 10 points, name this congress.

King Henry IV of France issued this decree in 1598 to give French Protestants known as Huguenots the right to worship in some places. It ended decades of religious wars. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685. For 10 points, name this edict, named for a city in western France.

After King Charles I was executed in 1649, this Puritan military leader ruled England without a king. He had led the New Model Army to victory in the English Civil War. He took the title Lord Protector in 1653. For 10 points, name this man.

text: This monument was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE on the west bank of the Nile. It was the tallest human-made structure in the world for thousands of years. It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still largely survives. For 10 points, name this largest pyramid at Giza.

In 49 BCE, this Roman general crossed the Rubicon River with his army and began a civil war. He became dictator for life and reformed the calendar. On the Ides of March in 44 BCE, he was stabbed by senators including Brutus and Cassius. For 10 points, name this Roman leader.

Born Gaius Octavius, this man was the grand-nephew and adopted heir of Julius Caesar. After defeating his rivals, he took a new name in 27 BCE and became Rome's first emperor. His long reign began the Pax Romana. For 10 points, name this ruler.

This woman was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt. She allied with Julius Caesar and later with Mark Antony. After her defeat in 31 BCE, she died by suicide, traditionally by the bite of an asp. For 10 points, name this queen of Egypt.

This king of Macedon took the throne at age twenty after his father Philip II was murdered. He defeated the Persian king Darius III at the battle of Gaugamela. He built an empire that reached as far as India before he died in Babylon in 323 BCE. For 10 points, name this conqueror.

This Greek city-state had two kings and a rigid military society. Boys began state training called the agoge at age seven. Its economy depended on enslaved helots who farmed the land. For 10 points, name this rival of Athens, a city in the Peloponnese.

Built in the fifth century BCE on the Acropolis, this temple honored the goddess Athena. The sculptor Phidias oversaw its decoration. Some of its marble sculptures are in the British Museum and are called the Elgin Marbles. For 10 points, name this Greek temple.

This Athenian philosopher taught by asking questions in a method named for him. He was convicted in 399 BCE of corrupting youth and failing to honor the city's gods. He drank poison hemlock rather than flee. For 10 points, name this teacher of Plato.

In about 1754 BCE, this king of Babylon had a collection of laws carved on a stone pillar. Its penalties often followed the principle of "an eye for an eye." The pillar was found in 1901 and now stands in the Louvre. For 10 points, name this ruler whose code is one of the oldest written legal codes.

French soldiers found this inscribed slab near the Nile delta in 1799. It carries the same decree written in hieroglyphs, a cursive Egyptian script, and Greek. Jean-Francois Champollion used it to decipher hieroglyphs. For 10 points, name this stone, now in the British Museum.

Howard Carter discovered the nearly intact tomb of this pharaoh in the Valley of the Kings in 1922. The young ruler took the throne as a boy and died around age eighteen. His golden death mask is world famous. For 10 points, name this "boy king" of Egypt.

Egyptian civilization grew along this river, whose yearly flood left rich black silt on its banks. It flows north through Egypt into the Mediterranean Sea. Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt were named for their positions along it. For 10 points, name this river.

The Sumerians pressed a reed stylus into wet clay to create this early system of writing. Its signs were wedge-shaped. It was used for languages including Akkadian and was eventually written on thousands of clay tablets in Mesopotamia. For 10 points, name this script.

Completed in 80 CE, this huge amphitheater in Rome could seat about fifty thousand spectators. It hosted gladiator fights and staged hunts. Its official name comes from the Flavian dynasty. For 10 points, name this ruined arena.

In 218 BCE, this general from Carthage led an army including war elephants across the Alps into Italy. He crushed the Romans at Cannae in 216 BCE. He was finally beaten at Zama in 202 BCE by Scipio Africanus. For 10 points, name this commander.

The first of these conflicts began over Sicily in 264 BCE. The second featured Hannibal's invasion of Italy. The third ended in 146 BCE with the destruction of Carthage. For 10 points, name these three wars between Rome and Carthage.

In 313, this emperor and Licinius issued the Edict of Milan, which granted tolerance to Christians. He won the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312. In 330 he dedicated a new capital on the site of Byzantium. For 10 points, name this emperor for whom that city was named.

In 79 CE, Mount Vesuvius buried this Roman city under volcanic ash. Its streets, shops, and even loaves of bread were preserved. Excavations began in the 1700s and show everyday life in the Roman Empire. For 10 points, name this city near Naples.

In 490 BCE, an Athenian army under Miltiades defeated a Persian invasion force on a plain northeast of Athens. According to legend, a runner carried news of the victory to the city. For 10 points, name this battle that gave its name to a long-distance race.

In 480 BCE, King Leonidas and about 300 Spartans held a narrow mountain pass against the huge army of Xerxes I. A local man named Ephialtes betrayed a path around them. The Greeks fought to the death while other forces retreated. For 10 points, name this battle.

This Athenian statesman led the city during its golden age and delivered a famous funeral oration. He promoted democracy and ordered the construction of the Parthenon. He died in a plague in 429 BCE. For 10 points, name this leader of Athens during its golden age.

In 539 BCE, this man captured Babylon and founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire. A clay cylinder describes his tolerant policies. He allowed exiled Jews to return to Jerusalem. For 10 points, name this Persian king whose title includes the word "Great."

This ruler unified China in 221 BCE and took a new title meaning "first emperor." He standardized writing, money, and weights and measures. He was buried near an army of thousands of life-size clay soldiers. For 10 points, name this founder of the Qin dynasty.

This network of trade routes linked China to the Mediterranean world during the Han dynasty. Caravans carried silk, spices, and paper west and gold and horses east. Ideas such as Buddhism also spread along it. For 10 points, name this system of routes named for a luxury fabric.

Held every four years in honor of Zeus, these athletic contests were traditionally first held in 776 BCE. They took place at a sanctuary in the Peloponnese. A modern revival began in Athens in 1896. For 10 points, name this athletic festival.

These seafaring traders came from cities such as Tyre and Sidon in present-day Lebanon. They were famous for purple dye made from sea snails. Their simple alphabet became the ancestor of the Greek alphabet and our own. For 10 points, name these people who founded Carthage.

Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were major cities of this Bronze Age civilization, which flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. It had planned streets laid out in grids and brick drains. Its script has never been deciphered. For 10 points, name this civilization of present-day Pakistan and India.

The historian Thucydides recorded this conflict, which lasted from 431 to 404 BCE. Pericles led Athens through its early years, and a plague killed thousands. It ended with Athens surrendering to a Spartan-led alliance. For 10 points, name this war between two Greek powers.

This Thracian gladiator escaped from a training school in Capua in 73 BCE and led a major slave rebellion. His army defeated several Roman forces before Marcus Licinius Crassus crushed it. Thousands of captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way. For 10 points, name this rebel leader.

In 31 BCE, Marcus Agrippa commanded the fleet of Octavian at this naval battle off the western coast of Greece. It defeated the forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. Octavian soon became the sole ruler of Rome. For 10 points, name this battle.

This emperor reigned from 284 to 305 and divided the empire's administration among four rulers in a system called the Tetrarchy. He launched the last great persecution of Christians. Unusually, he retired voluntarily to a palace on the Adriatic. For 10 points, name this Roman emperor.

This Byzantine emperor ordered a collection of Roman law that became the foundation of many European legal systems. He rebuilt the Hagia Sophia after the Nika riots and his generals, including Belisarius, reconquered parts of Italy and North Africa. His wife was Theodora. For 10 points, name this emperor.

Created around 450 BCE, this first written code of Roman law was posted publicly so that plebeians could know their rights. It was carved on bronze or wooden tablets and covered topics such as debt and family law. For 10 points, name this set of laws named for the number of tablets.

text: Born with the name Temujin, this leader united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and took a new title meaning "universal ruler." His cavalry conquered much of Central Asia and northern China. His descendants went on to build the largest contiguous land empire in history. For 10 points, name this Mongol leader who died in 1227.

This grandson of Genghis Khan completed the conquest of China and founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271. The Venetian traveler Marco Polo claimed to have served at his court. His attempts to invade Japan failed when storms destroyed his fleets. For 10 points, name this Mongol emperor.

This ruler of the Mali Empire made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and gave away so much gold that its price fell in Cairo. His reign made the city of Timbuktu a center of learning. For 10 points, name this wealthy West African king.

The Shona people built this large stone-walled city in southern Africa between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries. Its Great Enclosure has granite walls that were built without mortar. It gave its name to a modern country. For 10 points, name this archaeological site.

This island city in Lake Texcoco was the capital of the Aztec Empire. Causeways connected it to the mainland. After its fall in 1521 to Spanish forces, Mexico City was built on its ruins. For 10 points, name this city.

In 1519, this Spanish conquistador landed in Mexico with about 500 men. With help from native allies such as the Tlaxcalans, he captured the Aztec capital and the emperor Montezuma. For 10 points, name this explorer who conquered the Aztec Empire.

Machu Picchu was built in the Andes mountains by this empire, whose capital was Cusco. Its people kept records with knotted strings called quipus and built a vast network of roads. Francisco Pizarro captured its ruler Atahualpa in 1532. For 10 points, name this South American empire.

This Mesoamerican civilization built stepped pyramids at Chichen Itza and Tikal. Its scribes wrote in a system of glyphs and kept a complex calendar. The great cities of its Classic period in the southern lowlands declined around 900. For 10 points, name this civilization of the Yucatan and Guatemala.

This Venezuelan nicknamed "El Libertador" led armies that freed Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia from Spanish rule. He dreamed of a unified South America but saw it break apart. One country is named for him. For 10 points, name this leader.

This Indian leader used nonviolent civil disobedience, called satyagraha, to resist British rule. He was often called Mahatma, or "great soul." He was assassinated in New Delhi in January 1948. For 10 points, name this leader of the Indian independence movement.

In 1930, protesters led by Gandhi walked about 240 miles from Ahmedabad to the coastal village of Dandi. There he picked up a lump of natural salt in defiance of a British monopoly and tax. Thousands joined the nonviolent protest. For 10 points, name this campaign.

In 1868, a group of samurai and nobles restored the power of the emperor and ended the Tokugawa shogunate. The new government rapidly modernized Japan with railroads, a conscript army, and a constitution. For 10 points, name this transformation that took its name from an emperor.

This war began when Chinese official Lin Zexu destroyed chests of a drug seized from British merchants at Canton. Britain won, and the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842 gave it Hong Kong. For 10 points, name this war, fought over the trade in the drug from poppies.

The Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists, called "Boxers" by Westerners, led this uprising against foreigners and Christians in China from 1899 to 1901. Rebels besieged foreign legations in Beijing until an eight-nation army relieved them. For 10 points, name this rebellion.

This man's Long March of 1934 to 1935 took Communist forces to Shaanxi province. He proclaimed the People's Republic of China in 1949. His Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution caused enormous suffering. For 10 points, name this Communist leader of China.

This doctor founded the Kuomintang and served as the first provisional president of the Republic of China in 1912. He promoted the "Three Principles of the People": nationalism, democracy, and livelihood. For 10 points, name this man regarded as the "father" of modern China.

From its capital at Istanbul, this empire at its height controlled the Balkans, the Middle East, and North Africa. Its elite infantry were called Janissaries, and its rulers bore the title sultan. It lasted until 1922. For 10 points, name this Turkish empire.

This sultan reigned from 1520 to 1566 and led armies to the gates of Vienna in 1529. He was known in Turkey as "the Lawgiver" and sponsored the architect Sinan. For 10 points, name this Ottoman ruler whose epithet is "the Magnificent."

In May 1453, this young Ottoman sultan captured Constantinople after a siege in which huge cannons broke the city walls. He converted the Hagia Sophia into a mosque. His victory ended the Byzantine Empire. For 10 points, name this sultan nicknamed "the Conqueror."

This Kurdish sultan of Egypt and Syria defeated Crusaders at the Battle of Hattin in 1187 and recaptured Jerusalem. He later fought Richard the Lionheart in the Third Crusade. For 10 points, name this Muslim leader.

Born in Mecca around 570, this man received revelations that were recorded in the Quran. In 622 he made the Hijra, or migration, to Medina. Muslims consider him the final prophet. For 10 points, name this founder of Islam.

Shah Jahan built this white marble tomb in Agra in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Construction took about twenty years and was completed around 1653. Its design combines Persian, Islamic, and Indian styles. For 10 points, name this monument.

This Mughal emperor ruled from 1556 to 1605 and was the grandson of Babur. He conquered much of northern India and married Hindu princesses. He built a new capital at Fatehpur Sikri and promoted religious tolerance. For 10 points, name this ruler.

This uprising began in 1857 in Meerut when Indian soldiers in the British East India Company's army refused to use rifle cartridges rumored to be greased with animal fat. It spread across northern India. Afterward, Britain ended Company rule and ruled India directly. For 10 points, name this revolt.

In August 1947, British India was divided into two independent countries, one largely Hindu and one largely Muslim. Millions of people crossed the new border, and hundreds of thousands were killed in violence. For 10 points, name this division of South Asia.

This South African activist spent 27 years in prison, mostly on Robben Island, for fighting apartheid. After his release in 1990, he shared the Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk. In 1994 he became South Africa's first black president. For 10 points, name this man.

In 1948, South Africa's National Party formalized this system of racial segregation, whose name means "apartness" in Afrikaans. It forced people to live in separate areas and carry passes. It ended in the early 1990s. For 10 points, name this system of white minority rule.

This former enslaved man led the Haitian Revolution against French rule. He was captured by Napoleon's forces in 1802 and died in a French prison. His general Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared Haiti independent in 1804. For 10 points, name this Haitian leader.

This revolutionary overthrew Cuban dictator Fulgencio Batista in 1959. His government repelled the Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961 and allied with the Soviet Union. He ruled Cuba for decades. For 10 points, name this Cuban leader.

These warriors of feudal Japan followed a code of conduct called bushido. They served regional lords called daimyo and fought with swords called katana. The class was abolished after the Meiji Restoration. For 10 points, name this class of Japanese warriors.

In 1853, this American naval officer sailed four "black ships" into Edo Bay and demanded that Japan open to trade. The next year he signed the Treaty of Kanagawa. For 10 points, name this commodore who ended Japan's isolation.

This Zulu king built a powerful kingdom in southern Africa in the early 1800s. He introduced a short stabbing spear and reorganized his army into regiments. He was assassinated by his half-brothers in 1828. For 10 points, name this leader.

Opened in 1869 under the supervision of Ferdinand de Lesseps, this canal connected the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea. It shortened the sea route from Europe to Asia by avoiding the trip around Africa. For 10 points, name this Egyptian waterway.

Otto von Bismarck hosted this meeting of European powers in 1884 and 1885. Delegates set rules for dividing African territory among themselves. No African ruler was invited. For 10 points, name this conference that helped spark the "Scramble for Africa."

Between 1405 and 1433, this Chinese admiral commanded huge treasure fleets that sailed to India, Arabia, and East Africa. He served the Ming dynasty under the Yongle Emperor. For 10 points, name this eunuch and explorer.

text: In this novel, the title boy tricks his friends into whitewashing a fence for him and later witnesses a murder committed by Injun Joe. He is raised by his Aunt Polly in the town of Saint Petersburg and is sweet on Becky Thatcher. He and his friend Huck get lost in a cave and later find treasure. For 10 points, name this Mark Twain novel about a mischievous Missouri boy.

In this novel, a boy fakes his own death by killing a pig and splattering its blood in a cabin. The title character floats down a river with the escaped slave Jim, and meets two con men calling themselves the Duke and the King. He famously decides he will "go to hell" rather than turn Jim in. For 10 points, name this Mark Twain novel narrated by a boy raised by the Widow Douglas.

In this novel, Jess Aarons becomes friends with a new neighbor, Leslie Burke, after she beats the boys in a race. They build an imaginary kingdom in the woods across a creek, reached by swinging on a rope. Leslie dies when the rope breaks while Jess is away. For 10 points, name this Katherine Paterson novel about the kingdom of Terabithia.

The narrator of this novel, who asks to be called Ishmael, signs on to the whaling ship Pequod. The ship's captain has lost a leg and is obsessed with revenge, and the crew includes the harpooner Queequeg. It ends with a great white whale sinking the ship. For 10 points, name this novel by Herman Melville about Captain Ahab.

In this novel, Nick Carraway moves next door to a mysterious millionaire who throws lavish parties on Long Island. That millionaire stares at a green light at the end of a dock, hoping to win back Daisy Buchanan. It is set in the Jazz Age. For 10 points, name this F. Scott Fitzgerald novel about Jay Gatsby.

In this novel, a lawyer defends Tom Robinson, a Black man falsely accused of assault, in the town of Maycomb, Alabama. The story is narrated by his young daughter Scout, and her brother Jem. The reclusive Boo Radley saves the children from an attack. For 10 points, name this novel by Harper Lee.

In this novella, two migrant workers named George and Lennie dream of owning a farm where they can raise rabbits. Lennie, a gentle but very strong man, accidentally kills the wife of Curley. George makes a terrible decision beside a river at the end. For 10 points, name this short novel by John Steinbeck.

The narrator of this novel is expelled from Pencey Prep and wanders around New York City. He thinks most people are "phonies" and wants to protect children from falling off a cliff while playing in a field of rye. He has a sister named Phoebe. For 10 points, name this J. D. Salinger novel about Holden Caulfield.

In this novel, a Saint Bernard and Scottish shepherd mix named Buck is stolen from a California ranch and sold to be a sled dog. He joins the Klondike Gold Rush and eventually answers the call of his wolf ancestors. For 10 points, name this Jack London novel set in the Yukon.

This novel follows four sisters named Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy March, who grow up in Massachusetts while their father serves in the Civil War. Jo is an aspiring writer who cuts off her hair, and Beth dies of scarlet fever. For 10 points, name this novel by Louisa May Alcott.

The narrator of this novel is a greaser named Ponyboy Curtis, whose brother Darry looks after him after their parents die. After Johnny kills a Soc named Bob, Johnny and Ponyboy hide in an abandoned church. The poem "Nothing Gold Can Stay" is quoted in it. For 10 points, name this S. E. Hinton novel.

In this poem, a narrator mourns his lost Lenore while a visitor taps at his chamber door. A bird perched on a bust of Pallas says only one word in response to his questions. That word is "nevermore." For 10 points, name this poem by Edgar Allan Poe.

This poet wrote of a traveler who "took the one less traveled by" at a fork in a yellow wood. He also wrote "Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening" and "Fire and Ice." He recited a poem at John F. Kennedy's inauguration. For 10 points, name this New England poet of "The Road Not Taken."

This poet's collection Leaves of Grass included "Song of Myself" and was revised throughout his life. He wrote "O Captain! My Captain!" about the death of Abraham Lincoln. He worked as a nurse in the Civil War. For 10 points, name this American poet who celebrated himself and sang the body electric.

This poet of Amherst, Massachusetts wrote "Because I could not stop for Death" and "Hope is the thing with feathers." She rarely published during her life and used many dashes in her poems. Almost 1,800 of her poems were found after she died. For 10 points, name this reclusive poet.

This poet asked "What happens to a dream deferred?" in a poem that begins "Harlem." He also wrote "The Negro Speaks of Rivers." He was a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance. For 10 points, name this American poet.

This author's memoir I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings describes her childhood in Stamps, Arkansas. She read a poem at Bill Clinton's inauguration. She also wrote the poem "Still I Rise." For 10 points, name this American writer.

In this novella, an old Cuban fisherman named Santiago goes eighty-four days without catching a fish. He finally hooks a giant marlin and fights it for days, but sharks eat it on the way back to shore. For 10 points, name this short novel by Ernest Hemingway.
answer: The Old Man and the Sea

text: In this novel, the Joad family leaves their Oklahoma farm during the Dust Bowl and drives Route 66 to California. Tom Joad has just been released from prison, and Rose of Sharon gives birth to a stillborn baby. For 10 points, name this John Steinbeck novel.

In this novel, Guy Montag is a fireman whose job is to burn books. He meets a young neighbor named Clarisse and later escapes to join exiles who memorize books. The title is the temperature at which paper burns. For 10 points, name this dystopian novel by Ray Bradbury.

In this novel, a boy named Jonas is selected to be the Receiver of Memory in a community without color or pain. He learns about war, snow, and love, and later flees with a baby named Gabriel. For 10 points, name this Lois Lowry novel.

In this short story, the narrator insists he is not mad while describing how he killed an old man with a vulture-like eye. He hid the body under the floorboards but hears a heart beating louder and louder. For 10 points, name this Edgar Allan Poe story.

In this short story, a schoolteacher named Ichabod Crane is chased by a rider who throws a pumpkin at him. He competes with Brom Bones for the hand of Katrina Van Tassel. The title valley is near Tarrytown, New York. For 10 points, name this story by Washington Irving.

This play is set in 1692 Massachusetts, where girls led by Abigail Williams accuse villagers of witchcraft. John Proctor refuses to sign a false confession and is hanged. It is an allegory for McCarthyism. For 10 points, name this Arthur Miller play.

The Younger family in this play lives in a cramped Chicago apartment and debates how to spend a ten-thousand-dollar insurance check. Walter Lee wants to invest in a liquor store while his sister Beneatha wants to become a doctor. Its title comes from a Langston Hughes poem. For 10 points, name this Lorraine Hansberry play.

In this play, the Stage Manager narrates the lives of the people of Grover's Corners, New Hampshire. Emily Webb marries George Gibbs, then dies in childbirth and returns to relive one day. It is performed on a nearly bare stage. For 10 points, name this Thornton Wilder play.

In this novel, thirteen-year-old Brian Robeson survives alone in the Canadian wilderness after a plane crash. His only tool is a gift from his mother. For 10 points, name this Gary Paulsen novel named for a small axe.

In this novel, Stanley Yelnats is sent to Camp Green Lake, where boys must dig a hole five feet deep and five feet wide every day. He is cursed by his "no-good-dirty-rotten-pig-stealing-great-great-grandfather." He befriends Zero. For 10 points, name this Louis Sachar novel.

In this story, a lazy man falls asleep in the Catskill Mountains after drinking with strange men playing ninepins. He wakes up twenty years later with a long beard. For 10 points, name this Washington Irving story.

This book describes the author's two years living in a cabin near a Massachusetts pond. Chapters include "Economy," "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For," and "Sounds." Its author later wrote the essay "Civil Disobedience." For 10 points, name this work by Henry David Thoreau.

leadin: Answer these questions about Mark Twain.

parts.text: Mark Twain was the pen name of this man, who took the name from a riverboat term for water two fathoms deep.
In this Twain memoir, he recalls his days as a steamboat pilot on a great river.
In this Twain short story, Jim Smiley bets on a frog that has been filled with quail shot. Name this story set in Calaveras County.
parts.answer: The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County

leadin: Answer these questions about Edgar Allan Poe.

parts.text: Poe is often credited with inventing this genre of fiction through "The Murders in the Rue Morgue."
In this Poe story, a man bricks up his enemy Fortunato in a wine cellar. Name this story about a cask of wine.
This Poe story about Roderick and Madeline ends with a mansion splitting in two and falling into a tarn. Give its title.
parts.answer: The Fall of the House of Usher

leadin: Answer these questions about American poets.

parts.text: This poet and illustrator wrote the collection Where the Sidewalk Ends.
This Chicago poet wrote that "the fog comes on little cat feet."
This poet wrote "We Real Cool" and was the first Black author to win the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.

leadin: Answer these questions about American science fiction and fantasy.

parts.text: In this Madeleine L'Engle novel, Meg Murry travels through space to rescue her father using a tesseract.
In this Kurt Vonnegut novel, Billy Pilgrim becomes "unstuck in time" after surviving the bombing of Dresden.
Ray Bradbury wrote this book of linked stories about human colonists on a neighboring planet.

leadin: Answer these questions about the Transcendentalists.

parts.text: Walden Pond is near this Massachusetts town, where many Transcendentalists lived.
This Transcendentalist wrote the essays "Nature" and "Self-Reliance."
This woman edited the Transcendentalist journal The Dial and wrote Woman in the Nineteenth Century.

leadin: Answer these questions about American plays.

parts.text: This Arthur Miller play about the Loman family features a salesman named Willy.
This Tennessee Williams play features Blanche DuBois and her brother-in-law Stanley Kowalski.
This Tennessee Williams play about the Wingfield family features a collection of tiny glass animals.

leadin: Answer these questions about Ernest Hemingway.

parts.text: This Hemingway novel follows expatriates including Jake Barnes from Paris to the bullfights of Pamplona.
In this Hemingway novel, ambulance driver Frederic Henry falls in love with nurse Catherine Barkley during World War One.
In this Hemingway novel, an American named Robert Jordan fights alongside Spanish guerrillas. Its title comes from a John Donne meditation.

leadin: Answer these questions about American short stories.

parts.text: In this Shirley Jackson story, villagers gather each June to draw slips of paper from a black box.
In this O. Henry story, a young couple sells their most prized possessions, a watch and long hair, to buy each other Christmas presents.
In this Charlotte Perkins Gilman story, a woman confined to a room becomes obsessed with the pattern on its walls.

text: In this play, three witches tell a general that he will become king, and his wife urges him to murder the sleeping Duncan. He later sees a floating dagger and the ghost of Banquo. He is finally killed by Macduff after Birnam Wood seems to move. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare tragedy.

In this play, the fairy king Oberon tells Puck to put a love potion on the eyes of Demetrius. Titania falls in love with Bottom, whose head has been turned into a donkey's. A group of craftsmen performs "Pyramus and Thisbe." For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy set in a forest near Athens.

In this play, Cassius persuades Brutus to join a conspiracy against the ruler of Rome. A soothsayer warns the title character to beware the Ides of March. Mark Antony then delivers a speech that begins "Friends, Romans, countrymen." For 10 points, name this Shakespeare play in which the title character says "Et tu, Brute?"

In this play, Bassanio borrows money from Shylock with his friend Antonio as guarantor. Portia disguises herself as a lawyer and argues that the contract allows a pound of flesh but no blood. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare play set in an Italian city of canals.

This writer was born in Stratford-upon-Avon and married Anne Hathaway. His plays include comedies, histories, and tragedies, and he also wrote a sequence of 154 sonnets. He was a member of the Lord Chamberlain's Men. For 10 points, name this English playwright of Hamlet and Macbeth.

In this novel, an orphan raised in a workhouse famously asks, "Please, sir, I want some more." He falls in with Fagin and the Artful Dodger, who train boys as pickpockets. He is later threatened by Bill Sikes. For 10 points, name this Charles Dickens novel about a boy named Oliver.

In this novel, a blacksmith's apprentice named Pip is given money by a secret benefactor. He is cruelly treated by Estella, who is raised by Miss Havisham, a jilted bride who stopped all the clocks. The convict Magwitch turns out to be his benefactor. For 10 points, name this novel by Charles Dickens.

This novel opens with the line "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times." Set in London and Paris during the French Revolution, it features Madame Defarge, who knits the names of the doomed. Sydney Carton takes the place of Charles Darnay at the guillotine. For 10 points, name this Dickens novel.

In this novel, Elizabeth Bennet's first impression of the proud Mister Darcy is a bad one, and her sister Jane loves Mister Bingley. Lydia runs away with the soldier Wickham. It begins with the line that a single man with a fortune must want a wife. For 10 points, name this Jane Austen novel.

In this book, the animals of Manor Farm drive out Mister Jones and live by the Seven Commandments. The pigs Napoleon and Snowball fight for power, and the horse Boxer works himself to death. It ends with "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others." For 10 points, name this allegory by George Orwell.

In this novel, Jim Hawkins finds a map in the chest of the old pirate Billy Bones at the Admiral Benbow Inn. He sails on the Hispaniola and meets the one-legged cook Long John Silver. Ben Gunn has been marooned on the island. For 10 points, name this Robert Louis Stevenson adventure novel.

In this novella, the lawyer Mister Utterson investigates the connection between a respectable doctor and a vicious man who trampled a girl. The doctor has been drinking a chemical mixture that transforms him. For 10 points, name this Robert Louis Stevenson novella about a split personality.
answer: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
alternates: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

text: In this novel, a detective from Baker Street investigates the death of Sir Charles at Baskerville Hall on Dartmoor. A giant glowing creature is said to haunt the moor, but it is really a dog used by Stapleton. For 10 points, name this Arthur Conan Doyle novel starring Sherlock Holmes.

This fictional detective lives at 221B Baker Street and plays the violin. He is assisted by Doctor Watson and battles his enemy Professor Moriarty at the Reichenbach Falls. He is known for the line "Elementary." For 10 points, name this detective created by Arthur Conan Doyle.

In this novel, a man is shipwrecked and lives on an island for twenty-eight years. He saves a man from cannibals and names him for the day of the week on which he was found. For 10 points, name this Daniel Defoe novel about a castaway.

In this novel, Lemuel Gulliver visits Lilliput, where the people are six inches tall, and Brobdingnag, where they are giants. He later meets the intelligent horses called Houyhnhnms. For 10 points, name this satire by Jonathan Swift.

In this novel, Jonathan Harker visits a castle in Transylvania and later meets Van Helsing. Mina Harker is bitten by a count who sleeps in a coffin of earth. The novel is told through letters and diary entries. For 10 points, name this Bram Stoker novel.

In this novel, cylinders crash near Woking and release creatures from Mars who travel in giant tripod machines. The narrator watches them destroy London until they are killed by bacteria. For 10 points, name this H. G. Wells science fiction novel.

In this novel, an inventor travels to the year 802,701 and meets the gentle Eloi, who are preyed on by the Morlocks. He is helped by a young woman named Weena. For 10 points, name this H. G. Wells novel.

This theater was home to the Lord Chamberlain's Men and stood in London on the south bank of the Thames. A fire started by a cannon during a performance of Henry VIII destroyed the first one in 1613. For 10 points, name this circular theater where many Shakespeare plays premiered.

In this play, a professor of phonetics bets his friend Colonel Pickering that he can pass a Cockney flower girl off as a duchess. Eliza Doolittle learns to speak proper English. It was adapted as the musical My Fair Lady. For 10 points, name this George Bernard Shaw play.

In this collection of stories, a boy raised by wolves is taught the Law of the Jungle by the bear Baloo and the panther Bagheera. He is hunted by the tiger Shere Khan. For 10 points, name this Rudyard Kipling book about Mowgli.

In this play, Viola is shipwrecked in Illyria and disguises herself as the page Cesario. Countess Olivia falls for Viola, while Duke Orsino loves Olivia. Malvolio is tricked into wearing yellow stockings. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy.

This book was written by Sir Thomas Malory and printed by William Caxton. It tells of Lancelot, Guinevere, Merlin, and the Round Table. The title translates as "The Death of Arthur." For 10 points, name this French-titled collection of tales about the legendary king.

In this novel, a boy raised in Suffolk meets the kind Mister Micawber, the "umble" Uriah Heep, and his stern aunt Betsey Trotwood. He is friends with Steerforth and marries Dora. For 10 points, name this Dickens novel about a boy who becomes a writer.

In this novel, a handsome young man's portrait ages and grows hideous while he stays young. Lord Henry Wotton influences him, and the painter Basil Hallward is killed. For 10 points, name this Oscar Wilde novel about a man named Dorian.

This novel is set in a future World State in which babies are grown in bottles and sorted into castes such as Alphas and Epsilons. The citizens take a drug called soma, and a man called the Savage is brought from a reservation. For 10 points, name this Aldous Huxley dystopian novel.

In this poem, the speaker sees a "crowd, a host, of golden" flowers beside a lake, fluttering and dancing in the breeze. It was inspired by a walk in the Lake District. For 10 points, name this poem by William Wordsworth that begins "I wandered lonely as a cloud."
answer: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud

text: In this poem, a sailor stops a wedding guest and tells him about a voyage. After he shoots a large seabird, the ship is becalmed, and he laments "Water, water, every where." For 10 points, name this Samuel Taylor Coleridge poem about a sailor who is cursed.
answer: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

text: This poem begins "Tyger Tyger, burning bright, in the forests of the night." It asks what immortal hand or eye could frame the animal's fearful symmetry. It is a companion to "The Lamb." For 10 points, name this William Blake poem about a large cat.

leadin: Answer these questions about Shakespeare's tragedies.

parts.text: This Shakespeare play features a prince of Denmark and the line "To be, or not to be."
In this Shakespeare play, an aging king divides his kingdom among his daughters Goneril and Regan, but disowns Cordelia.
In this Shakespeare play, Iago manipulates a Moorish general into thinking his wife Desdemona has been unfaithful.

leadin: Answer these questions about Jane Austen.

parts.text: In this Austen novel, a matchmaking young woman from Highbury meddles in the love lives of her friends.
In this Austen novel, the sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood experience heartbreak.
In this Austen novel, Catherine Morland imagines a Gothic mystery at a certain abbey.

leadin: Answer these questions about Romantic poets.

parts.text: This poet wrote "Ozymandias," about a ruined statue in the desert.
This poet wrote "Ode on a Grecian Urn" and "To Autumn" before dying young of tuberculosis.
This poet of the Victorian era wrote "The Charge of the Light Brigade" and "Ulysses."

leadin: Answer these questions about Shakespearean characters.

parts.text: This wife of a Scottish thane urges her husband to murder the king and later cannot wash imaginary blood from her hands.
This villain of Othello is the general's ensign who plots his downfall.
This fat, boastful knight is a friend of Prince Hal in the Henry IV plays and appears in The Merry Wives of Windsor.

leadin: Answer these questions about George Eliot.

parts.text: George Eliot was the pen name of this woman.
In this Eliot novel set in a provincial town, Dorothea Brooke marries the scholar Casaubon.
In this Eliot novel, a weaver in Raveloe finds a golden-haired child by his fire after his gold is stolen.

leadin: Answer these questions about Thomas Hardy.

parts.text: In this Hardy novel, a poor girl from Wessex is seduced by Alec and later marries Angel Clare.
In this Hardy novel, a stonemason named Jude Fawley dreams of studying at a university city called Christminster.
In this Hardy novel, Michael Henchard sells his wife and later becomes the mayor of a Dorset town.

leadin: Answer these questions about early English writers.

parts.text: This man wrote The Canterbury Tales.
This Elizabethan playwright wrote Doctor Faustus and Tamburlaine.
This blind poet wrote Paradise Lost.

leadin: Answer these questions about Agatha Christie.

parts.text: Christie created this Belgian detective with a waxed mustache.
In this Christie novel, Poirot investigates a murder aboard a train stopped by a snowdrift.
In this Christie novel, ten strangers are lured to Soldier Island and killed one by one.

text: In this novel, an aging Spanish gentleman reads so many tales of chivalry that he renames his horse Rocinante and sets out as a knight. He attacks windmills that he believes are giants and is accompanied by his squire Sancho Panza. He dedicates his deeds to Dulcinea. For 10 points, name this novel by Miguel de Cervantes.

In this novel, Jean Valjean is imprisoned for nineteen years for stealing a loaf of bread and is relentlessly pursued by the inspector Javert. He adopts Cosette, the daughter of Fantine. The story climaxes at a barricade during the 1832 Paris uprising. For 10 points, name this novel by Victor Hugo.

In this novel, the bell ringer Quasimodo is deaf and deformed and lives in a cathedral in Paris. He rescues the Gypsy dancer Esmeralda from the archdeacon Claude Frollo. For 10 points, name this Victor Hugo novel set at Notre-Dame.

In this novel, the young Gascon d'Artagnan travels to Paris and befriends Athos, Porthos, and Aramis. They battle the forces of Cardinal Richelieu and the spy Milady de Winter. Their motto is "All for one, and one for all." For 10 points, name this Alexandre Dumas novel.

In this novel, a young sailor named Edmond Dantès is falsely imprisoned in the Château d'If. He learns of a hidden treasure from the Abbé Faria and later takes revenge under a noble title. For 10 points, name this Alexandre Dumas novel about a man who becomes a wealthy count.
In this novel, Professor Aronnax, his servant Conseil, and the harpooner Ned Land are captured by Captain Nemo. They travel in the submarine Nautilus. For 10 points, name this Jules Verne novel.
answer: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea

text: In this novel, Phileas Fogg wagers fellow members of the Reform Club that he can circle the globe in the time given in the title. He travels with his servant Passepartout and is trailed by the detective Fix. For 10 points, name this Jules Verne novel.
answer: Around the World in Eighty Days

text: In this book, a pilot crashes in the Sahara and meets a boy from a tiny asteroid. The boy talks about a rose he loves and a fox who asks to be tamed. It contains the line "What is essential is invisible to the eye." For 10 points, name this novella by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry.

These two German brothers, Jacob and Wilhelm, collected tales from storytellers and published them as Children's and Household Tales. Their collection includes "Rumpelstiltskin," "Snow White," and "Rapunzel." For 10 points, name these scholars of fairy tales.

In this fairy tale, a little girl named Gerda sets out to rescue her friend Kai, who has a splinter of a troll's mirror in his eye. They are separated by a ruler of a frozen palace. For 10 points, name this Hans Christian Andersen tale that inspired a Disney film.

In this fairy tale, two swindlers claim to weave cloth that is invisible to people who are unfit for their jobs. A child in a crowd finally says the ruler has nothing on. For 10 points, name this Hans Christian Andersen story.

In this fairy tale, an odd baby bird is mocked by the farm animals because he is big and gray. After a hard winter, he sees his reflection and realizes he is a swan. For 10 points, name this Hans Christian Andersen story.

In this novella, a traveling salesman wakes up one morning transformed into a giant insect. His sister Grete eventually stops caring for him, and his father throws apples at him. For 10 points, name this story about Gregor Samsa by Franz Kafka.

This novel follows the Rostov and Bolkonsky families during the French invasion of Russia in 1812. Characters include the idealistic Pierre Bezukhov, Prince Andrei, and Natasha. For 10 points, name this very long novel by Leo Tolstoy.

In this novel, a woodcarver named Geppetto carves a puppet that comes to life. The puppet's nose grows when he lies, and he is swallowed by a sea creature. His conscience is a talking cricket. For 10 points, name this novel by Carlo Collodi.

In this play, a swordsman with a huge nose helps the handsome Christian win the love of Roxane by writing letters in his name. He dies after being hit on the head by a log. For 10 points, name this Edmond Rostand play about a poet and soldier.

In this novel, an orphan girl is sent to live with her grandfather in the Swiss Alps and befriends the goatherd Peter. She is later taken to Frankfurt to keep company with Clara, who uses a wheelchair. For 10 points, name this Johanna Spyri novel about a girl.

The title girl of this book has red braids, super strength, and a horse. She lives at Villa Villekulla with a monkey named Mister Nilsson, and befriends Tommy and Annika. For 10 points, name this Astrid Lindgren book series about a Swedish girl.

In this novel, a masked figure lives beneath the Paris Opera House and tutors the singer Christine Daaé. He drops a chandelier and loves Christine despite her love for Raoul. For 10 points, name this Gaston Leroux novel.

This book was written by a Jewish girl who hid in a secret annex above her father's office in Amsterdam. She addressed entries to an imaginary friend named Kitty. For 10 points, name this diary by Anne Frank.
answer: The Diary of a Young Girl

text: In this novel by Johann Wyss, a shipwrecked pastor and his wife and four sons build a home in a giant tree on a tropical island. The father narrates their efforts to survive with animals and plants. For 10 points, name this novel about a stranded family.

In this story by E. T. A. Hoffmann, Marie receives a wooden toy from her godfather Drosselmeier. The toy comes to life and defeats the Mouse King. Tchaikovsky based a famous ballet on it. For 10 points, name this Christmas story about a toy soldier who cracks nuts.
alternates: The Nutcracker and the Mouse King

text: In this novel by Michael Ende, a boy named Bastian steals a book from a bookstore and reads it in his school attic. He is pulled into the land of Fantasia and aids the young warrior Atreyu. For 10 points, name this German children's fantasy that features a luckdragon named Falkor.

In this novel, Paul Bäumer and his classmates enlist after a teacher's patriotic speeches. They face death at the front in World War One. It ends as Paul is killed on a day when the army report notes nothing new. For 10 points, name this Erich Maria Remarque novel.
answer: All Quiet on the Western Front

text: This Finnish author wrote and illustrated books about a family of white trolls living in a valley, including Finn Family Moomintroll. The characters include Snufkin and Little My. For 10 points, name this author of the Moomin series.

In this short story by Nikolai Gogol, a poor clerk named Akaky Akakievich saves for months to buy a new garment. It is stolen, and he dies after a powerful person refuses to help him. His ghost then snatches coats in Saint Petersburg. For 10 points, name this story named for a piece of clothing.

This seventeenth-century French author collected fairy tales such as "Cinderella," "Puss in Boots," and "Sleeping Beauty." His book was published as Tales of Mother Goose. For 10 points, name this author who gave Cinderella her glass slipper.

This series of comic albums by the Belgian artist Hergé follows a young reporter with a tuft of hair. His dog is Snowy, and his friends include Captain Haddock and Professor Calculus. For 10 points, name this reporter whose adventures include The Blue Lotus.

This comic series by René Goscinny and Albert Uderzo follows a Gaulish village that resists Roman conquest. The warriors drink a magic potion brewed by the druid Getafix. The hero's large friend Obelix carries menhirs. For 10 points, name this series about a small warrior.

In this fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm, a brother and sister leave a trail of breadcrumbs that birds eat. They find a house made of sweets and escape a witch by pushing her into an oven. For 10 points, name this fairy tale.

leadin: Answer these questions about Russian authors.

parts.text: This author wrote Anna Karenina, which begins with a line about happy and unhappy families.
This author's novel Crime and Punishment follows Raskolnikov, a student who murders a pawnbroker.
This playwright wrote The Cherry Orchard and Three Sisters.

leadin: Answer these questions about French authors.

parts.text: This Enlightenment writer wrote Candide, a satire in which a young man is taught that this is the best of all possible worlds.
This Algerian-born author wrote The Stranger and The Plague and won the Nobel Prize in 1957.
This author wrote the seven-volume novel In Search of Lost Time, and is famous for the narrator tasting a madeleine dipped in tea.

leadin: Answer these questions about German authors.

parts.text: This author wrote the play Faust and the novel The Sorrows of Young Werther.
This author wrote Death in Venice and The Magic Mountain.
This author wrote Siddhartha and Steppenwolf.

leadin: Answer these questions about Scandinavian writers.

parts.text: This Danish author wrote "The Little Mermaid."
This Norwegian playwright wrote A Doll's House, in which Nora leaves her husband.
This Swedish playwright wrote Miss Julie and The Dance of Death.

leadin: Answer these questions about Spanish writers.

parts.text: This author wrote Don Quixote.
This poet and dramatist wrote Blood Wedding and Poet in New York and was killed at the start of the Spanish Civil War.
This seventeenth-century dramatist wrote Life Is a Dream.

leadin: Answer these questions about Italian writers.

parts.text: This author of the Divine Comedy is guided through hell by Virgil.
This author wrote the Decameron, in which ten young people tell stories to escape the plague in Florence.
This poet wrote a sequence of sonnets to a woman named Laura.

leadin: Answer these questions about Jules Verne.

parts.text: In this Verne novel, Professor Lidenbrock and his nephew Axel descend into a volcano in Iceland.
parts.answer: Journey to the Center of the Earth
alternates: A Journey to the Center of the Earth

parts.text: In this Verne novel, three men are fired toward the lunar surface from a giant cannon.
parts.answer: From the Earth to the Moon

parts.text: In this Verne novel, a group of balloonists from the American Civil War end up on an island with Captain Nemo.

leadin: Answer these questions about European folk tales.

parts.text: In this tale, a musician in a colorful coat lures rats from a town in Lower Saxony with his pipe, then leads away the children when he is not paid.
In this Grimm tale, a donkey, a dog, a cat, and a rooster set out to become musicians and scare off robbers.
In this French tale, a wealthy man with a strange-colored facial hair kills his wives and forbids the latest to open a certain room.

text: In this novel, Okonkwo is a proud wrestler in the Igbo village of Umuofia who accidentally kills a clansman. After being exiled, he returns to find that British missionaries and colonial officials have changed his community. His son Nwoye converts to Christianity. For 10 points, name this novel by Chinua Achebe.

In this novel, an Andalusian shepherd boy named Santiago has a recurring dream about treasure near the Pyramids. He meets a king named Melchizedek, falls in love with Fatima in the desert, and learns to listen to his heart. For 10 points, name this novel by the Brazilian author Paulo Coelho.

In this collection, a queen named Scheherazade tells her husband a story every night so that he will not execute her. The stories include the voyages of Sinbad the Sailor. For 10 points, name this collection of Middle Eastern folk tales, whose title includes the number one thousand and one.

In this novel, Amir betrays his friend Hassan, a Hazara servant, during a kite-fighting tournament in Kabul. Years later, he returns to Afghanistan to rescue Hassan's son Sohrab. For 10 points, name this novel by Khaled Hosseini.

This graphic memoir follows the author as a girl in Tehran during the Islamic Revolution. She is later sent to school in Vienna. It was written and drawn in black and white by Marjane Satrapi. For 10 points, name this autobiographical comic.

In this novel, a boy named Piscine Molitor Patel survives a shipwreck on a lifeboat with a Bengal tiger named Richard Parker. Its author is the Canadian writer Yann Martel. For 10 points, name this novel about a boy adrift in the Pacific.

This memoir recounts how a teenager and his father, Shlomo, survive the concentration camps at Auschwitz and Buchenwald. It begins in the town of Sighet in Transylvania. For 10 points, name this short book by Elie Wiesel.

In this Chinese novel, the monk Xuanzang travels to India to retrieve Buddhist scriptures. He is protected by Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, along with Pigsy and Sandy. For 10 points, name this novel attributed to Wu Cheng'en.

This work, written by the court lady Murasaki Shikibu, is often called one of the world's first novels. It follows the "Shining Prince" and is set in the Heian court of Japan. For 10 points, name this work named for its hero, Hikaru.

In this Sanskrit epic, Prince Rama is exiled to the forest with his wife Sita and brother Lakshmana. Sita is kidnapped by the demon king Ravana, and Rama enlists the monkey god Hanuman to rescue her. For 10 points, name this Hindu epic attributed to Valmiki.

In this Mesopotamian epic, the king of Uruk becomes friends with the wild man Enkidu and battles the monster Humbaba. After Enkidu dies, the hero seeks the immortal Utnapishtim, who survived a great flood. For 10 points, name this epic about a Sumerian king.

This sacred book of the K'iche' Maya tells of the Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, who defeat the lords of the underworld Xibalba. It also describes how humans were created from maize. For 10 points, name this Mayan text of Guatemala.
This Chilean poet wrote Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair and many odes to common things like socks and tomatoes. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971. For 10 points, name this poet.

This thirteenth-century Persian poet founded the Mevlevi order, whose followers whirl in a ritual dance. He wrote the Masnavi and lived in Konya. For 10 points, name this mystic poet whose verses are widely read in English translation.

This collection of quatrains was written by a Persian mathematician and astronomer and translated into English by Edward FitzGerald. It includes the line "A Jug of Wine, a Loaf of Bread, and Thou." For 10 points, name this work of Omar Khayyam.

In this Latin epic, the hero flees the burning city of Troy and lands in Carthage, where Queen Dido falls in love with him. He fights Turnus in Italy. For 10 points, name this epic by Virgil that tells of the founding of Rome.

In this Greek tragedy, a plague strikes Thebes, and the king learns that he killed his father and married his mother. Jocasta hangs herself, and the king blinds himself. For 10 points, name this play by Sophocles.

This ancient Greek storyteller is credited with fables such as "The Tortoise and the Hare" and "The Boy Who Cried Wolf." Each of his tales ends with a moral. For 10 points, name this legendary author.

In this novel, the Zulu minister Stephen Kumalo travels from his village to Johannesburg to search for his son Absalom. It was published in 1948. For 10 points, name this novel whose title is a plea for a land.

In this memoir, a comedian describes growing up in South Africa during apartheid as the son of a Black mother and a white father. His mother Patricia is a major figure. For 10 points, name this book by Trevor Noah whose title refers to the illegality of his birth.

In this memoir, a girl from the Swat Valley of Pakistan describes being shot by the Taliban for speaking out about girls' education. It was coauthored with Christina Lamb. For 10 points, name this book by a Nobel Peace Prize winner.

In this Mexican novel, Tita is forbidden to marry Pedro and pours her emotions into cooking. Each chapter begins with a recipe. For 10 points, name this novel by Laura Esquivel whose title describes water at the point of boiling.

This seventeenth-century Japanese poet perfected the haiku and wrote a travel diary called The Narrow Road to the Deep North. His most famous poem describes a frog jumping into an old pond. For 10 points, name this poet.

This Bengali writer won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 for his collection Gitanjali. He founded a school at Santiniketan and wrote the lyrics of the national anthems of India and Bangladesh. For 10 points, name this poet.

This Sanskrit epic, attributed to Vyasa, is one of the longest poems ever written. It tells of a war at Kurukshetra between the Pandavas and the Kauravas. It contains the Bhagavad Gita. For 10 points, name this Indian epic.

This eighteenth-century Chinese novel follows the decline of the Jia family. It features Jia Baoyu and Lin Daiyu and is also called The Story of the Stone. For 10 points, name this novel by Cao Xueqin.
alternates: The Dream of the Red Chamber

text: In this memoir, a twelve-year-old girl in Shanghai wants to join the Red Successors but her family is labeled as having a bad background. It describes the Cultural Revolution. For 10 points, name this memoir by Ji-li Jiang.

In this novel, Mariam and Laila become wives of the abusive Rasheed in Kabul. It follows the two women through decades of conflict in Afghanistan. For 10 points, name this novel by Khaled Hosseini whose title is from a poem.

This ancient Greek poet, traditionally said to have been blind, composed two epics about the Trojan War and its aftermath. They feature the heroes Achilles and Odysseus. For 10 points, name this poet.

This autobiography describes how the author grew up in a Xhosa village, became a lawyer, and was sentenced at the Rivonia Trial. He spent years on Robben Island before becoming president of South Africa. For 10 points, name this memoir by Nelson Mandela.

leadin: Answer these questions about Greek dramatists.

parts.text: This tragedian wrote Medea, in which a woman takes revenge on Jason.
This author wrote the Oresteia trilogy, which includes Agamemnon.
This comic playwright wrote Lysistrata and The Frogs.

leadin: Answer these questions about African writers.

parts.text: This author wrote Things Fall Apart and was born in the Igbo town of Ogidi.
This Nigerian playwright won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986 and wrote Death and the King's Horseman.
This Kenyan author wrote Weep Not, Child and A Grain of Wheat, and for years wrote in the Gikuyu language.

text: In this novel, Gandalf and thirteen dwarves led by Thorin Oakenshield recruit a homebody to help reclaim a treasure guarded by a dragon. The hero wins a magic ring in a riddle contest with Gollum. For 10 points, name this novel by J. R. R. Tolkien about Bilbo Baggins.

In this novel, four siblings enter a magical land through a wardrobe in a professor's house. Edmund betrays the others for Turkish delight, and the White Witch keeps the land in perpetual winter. A lion sacrifices himself at the Stone Table. For 10 points, name this book by C. S. Lewis, the first published in the Chronicles of Narnia.
answer: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe
alternates: Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

text: In this novel, a girl follows a white rabbit with a pocket watch down a hole. She attends a tea party with the Mad Hatter, plays croquet with flamingos, and meets a Queen who shouts "Off with her head!" For 10 points, name this Lewis Carroll novel.

In this play, Wendy, John, and Michael Darling fly with the title boy to the Neverland. They fight the pirate Captain Hook, who is chased by a crocodile that swallowed a clock. Tinker Bell drinks poison meant for the hero. For 10 points, name this J. M. Barrie play about a boy who never grows up.

In this novel, Charlie Bucket wins one of five golden tickets to tour a factory run by Willy Wonka. Other winners include Augustus Gloop and Veruca Salt. The Oompa-Loompas work in the factory. For 10 points, name this Roald Dahl novel about a sweet-making plant.

In this novel, a brilliant girl reads at a library and discovers she can move objects with her mind. She is mistreated by her car-salesman father and by the headmistress Miss Trunchbull. Miss Honey is her kindly teacher. For 10 points, name this Roald Dahl novel.

In this book, a boy named Christopher Robin lives with a bear who loves honey and has a friend named Piglet. Other animals in the Hundred Acre Wood include Eeyore and Tigger. For 10 points, name this A. A. Milne book about a bear of very little brain.

In this novel, a Mole meets a Water Rat, and they have adventures with Badger and a rich, reckless amphibian who loves motor cars. Toad Hall is eventually retaken from weasels. For 10 points, name this Kenneth Grahame novel set on a riverbank.

In this novel, Mary Lennox is sent from India to live at Misselthwaite Manor in Yorkshire. She finds a locked, overgrown garden and befriends Dickon and her sickly cousin Colin. For 10 points, name this Frances Hodgson Burnett novel.
In this book, a mischievous bunny wearing a blue jacket sneaks into Mister McGregor's garden. His siblings are Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cottontail. For 10 points, name this Beatrix Potter book.

In this picture book, Max is sent to bed without supper after wearing a wolf suit. He sails to an island and becomes king of creatures with terrible claws. Max says "Let the wild rumpus start!" For 10 points, name this Maurice Sendak book.

In this picture book, a tiny creature hatches from an egg on a Sunday and eats through one apple on Monday, two pears on Tuesday, and so on. After a stomachache, it forms a cocoon. For 10 points, name this Eric Carle book.

In this novel, a boy discovers he is the son of Poseidon and is accused of stealing Zeus's master bolt. He attends Camp Half-Blood with Annabeth and Grover. For 10 points, name this Rick Riordan novel, the first in the Percy Jackson series.
alternates: Percy Jackson and the Lightning Thief
Percy Jackson and the Olympians: The Lightning Thief

text: In this novel, Katniss Everdeen volunteers to take her sister Prim's place in a televised fight to the death. She represents District 12 alongside Peeta Mellark. For 10 points, name this Suzanne Collins novel set in Panem.

In this novel, Frodo Baggins inherits a ring and sets out with eight companions to destroy it in the fires of Mount Doom. Sauron is its dark lord. For 10 points, name this epic fantasy trilogy by J. R. R. Tolkien.

In this novel, a boy named August Pullman, who has a facial difference, starts fifth grade at Beecher Prep. His teacher Mister Browne teaches precepts, including that one should choose kindness. For 10 points, name this R. J. Palacio novel.

This novel is narrated by a horse who describes his early life on a farm and his hard years pulling cabs in London. His friends include Ginger and Merrylegs. For 10 points, name this Anna Sewell novel.
This sound device repeats the same consonant sound at the start of nearby words. "Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers" is a tongue twister that uses it. For 10 points, name this device.
"I've told you a million times" and "I'm so hungry I could eat a horse" are examples of this figure of speech. It uses deliberate exaggeration for emphasis. For 10 points, name this figure of speech.
This fourteen-line poem is written in iambic pentameter. The Petrarchan form has an octave and a sestet, while Shakespeare's form ends with a rhyming couplet. For 10 points, name this form of poem.
This five-line humorous poem has an AABBA rhyme scheme and is often nonsense. Edward Lear popularized it. For 10 points, name this form that can begin "There once was a man from Nantucket."

In its verbal form, a speaker says the opposite of what is meant. In its situational form, an outcome is the reverse of what is expected. In its dramatic form, the audience knows something that a character does not. For 10 points, name this literary device.
This device uses hints early in a story to suggest what will happen later. An author might use a storm cloud or a character's omen to create it. For 10 points, name this narrative technique.

In literature, this term refers to the main character of a story, who is often opposed by an antagonist. The word comes from Greek for "first actor." For 10 points, name this term for a story's central character.

In this kind of story, the characters, settings, and events represent ideas such as virtue or vice. Pilgrim's Progress is a famous example. For 10 points, name this type of narrative with a hidden symbolic meaning.

In this genre, authors imagine a society in which people suffer under oppressive control, as in The Giver and Fahrenheit 451. It is the opposite of a utopia. For 10 points, name this genre of science fiction.
