text: This organelle has a double membrane, contains its own small circular DNA, and carries out most of the steps of cellular respiration. Its inner membrane is folded into cristae. For 10 points, name this "powerhouse of the cell" that makes most of its ATP.

This molecule is found in the nucleus and is shaped like a twisted ladder, or double helix. Its rungs are made of the base pairs adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine. Watson and Crick described its structure in 1953. For 10 points, name this molecule that carries genetic information.

Cells of this kind lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Their DNA floats in a region called the nucleoid, and they include the domains Bacteria and Archaea. For 10 points, name this simple type of cell, contrasted with eukaryotic cells.

This process takes place in chloroplasts. It uses light energy, water, and carbon dioxide to make glucose and releases oxygen as a byproduct. For 10 points, name this process by which plants make their own food.

In this stage of the cell cycle, a cell grows and copies its DNA before it divides. It makes up the majority of the time in the life of a typical cell. For 10 points, name this stage that comes before mitosis.

These proteins act as biological catalysts, speeding up chemical reactions in living things without being used up. Amylase and lactase are examples, and each one fits a specific substrate at its active site. For 10 points, name these proteins whose names usually end in "-ase."

This system of the human body includes the heart, blood vessels, and blood. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, while veins return it. For 10 points, name this system that transports oxygen and nutrients around the body.

This is the term for the passive movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from an area of low solute concentration to an area of high solute concentration. A cell placed in pure water will swell because of it. For 10 points, name this process.

Gregor Mendel studied inheritance by crossing varieties of this plant in a monastery garden. He tracked traits such as seed shape and flower color. For 10 points, name this plant, whose pods hold the seeds Mendel counted.

In this kind of cell division, one cell divides to make two genetically identical daughter cells with the same number of chromosomes. Its phases are prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase. For 10 points, name this process used for growth and repair of body tissues.

This is the green pigment found in chloroplasts that absorbs mostly red and blue light. It reflects green light, which is why leaves look green. For 10 points, name this pigment essential to photosynthesis.

This organelle is surrounded by a double membrane called an envelope that is perforated by pores. It contains the chromatin and a dense region called the nucleolus, where ribosomes are assembled. For 10 points, name this organelle that houses most of a eukaryotic cell's DNA.

These structures are made of ribosomal RNA and protein and are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. They may float free in the cytoplasm or attach to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. For 10 points, name these tiny structures where translation builds proteins.

A typical example of this process begins with an enzyme called helicase that unzips the double helix. DNA polymerase then adds complementary nucleotides to each strand. Because each new molecule keeps one old strand, it is called semiconservative. For 10 points, name this process in which DNA is copied.

This is the term for a pair of alleles that are identical, such as AA or aa. Organisms with this condition are said to be pure for the trait. For 10 points, name this genetic condition, the opposite of heterozygous.

Stacks of flattened sacs called cisternae make up this organelle, which receives vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum. It modifies, sorts, and packages proteins for secretion. For 10 points, name this organelle named for an Italian scientist who described it in 1898.

In this process, the sequence of a gene is used to build a strand of messenger RNA by the enzyme RNA polymerase. It occurs in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells. For 10 points, name this first step of gene expression, which comes before translation.

Hemoglobin in these cells carries oxygen. Mature ones in humans have no nucleus and are shaped like biconcave disks. For 10 points, name these cells, also called erythrocytes, that give blood its red color.

This kingdom includes mushrooms, molds, and yeasts. Its members have cell walls made of chitin and absorb nutrients from their surroundings. For 10 points, name this kingdom of organisms that are neither plants nor animals.

Charles Darwin visited these Pacific islands on the HMS Beagle and observed finches and tortoises that differed from island to island. These observations helped shape his theory of natural selection. For 10 points, name these islands belonging to Ecuador.

In this process, water moves up a plant and evaporates from tiny pores on the underside of leaves. The pores are called stomata and are controlled by guard cells. For 10 points, name this loss of water vapor from plants.

This kind of relationship benefits both species involved. Examples include bees pollinating flowers and the bacteria in your gut that help digest food. For 10 points, name this kind of symbiosis, contrasted with parasitism and commensalism.

The Punnett square is used to predict the results of genetic crosses. If two heterozygous parents, Bb and Bb, are crossed, the expected ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes is this. For 10 points, give this ratio.

These tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles are where gas exchange takes place in the lungs. They are surrounded by networks of capillaries. For 10 points, name these structures where oxygen enters the blood.

This structure of the cell is a fluid mosaic made of a bilayer of phospholipids with embedded proteins. The heads of its molecules are hydrophilic and the tails are hydrophobic. Cholesterol helps regulate its fluidity. For 10 points, name this boundary that controls what enters and leaves a cell.

This cycle is also called the citric acid cycle. It takes place in the mitochondrial matrix, where acetyl CoA combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate. It produces NADH, FADH2, and carbon dioxide. For 10 points, name this cycle named for a German-British biochemist.

The Hardy-Weinberg principle describes how common gene variants are in a population that is not evolving. Its equation is p squared plus 2pq plus q squared equals one, where p and q stand for these quantities. For 10 points, name these two things whose frequencies sum to one in the equation p plus q equals one.

These organelles in animal cells are filled with digestive enzymes and work at an acidic pH. A disease such as Tay-Sachs results when one of their enzymes is missing. For 10 points, name these organelles that break down worn-out cell parts and ingested material.

This type of cell division produces four haploid cells from one diploid cell. Crossing over occurs during its first prophase, and homologous chromosomes separate in its first anaphase. For 10 points, name this cell division that produces gametes.

Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments helped disprove this old idea, the notion that living things can arise from nonliving matter. For 10 points, name this idea, which Francesco Redi also tested with jars of meat and flies.

text: This element has atomic number 1 and is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe. Two atoms of it bond with one of oxygen to form water. For 10 points, name this element with the symbol H.

This noble gas is used to fill balloons because it is lighter than air and does not burn. It is the second lightest element and has atomic number 2. For 10 points, name this gas, which makes a person's voice squeaky when inhaled.

This scale runs from 0 to 14 and measures how acidic or basic a solution is. Pure water sits at 7 on it, lemon juice is far lower, and household bleach is far higher. Litmus paper and universal indicator are used to estimate readings on it. For 10 points, name this scale.

The three states of matter most often seen on Earth are solid, liquid, and this one. Particles of it are far apart, move quickly, and fill any container. For 10 points, name this state of matter that includes air.
In this kind of bond, two atoms share pairs of electrons. Water molecules and methane molecules are held together by it. For 10 points, name this type of bond, contrasted with the ionic type.

This is the smallest particle of an element that still has the properties of that element. It has a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons. For 10 points, name this basic unit of matter.

Table salt, whose formula is NaCl, is made of sodium and this other element. This yellow-green gas is a poisonous halogen with atomic number 17. It is added in small amounts to swimming pools and drinking water to kill germs. For 10 points, name this element.

This is the process in which a solid turns directly into a gas without becoming a liquid first. Dry ice does this at room temperature, and so does snow on a cold, dry, sunny day. The reverse process is called deposition. For 10 points, name this change of state.
This metal is liquid at room temperature and was once used in thermometers. Its symbol Hg comes from a Latin name meaning "liquid silver." For 10 points, name this element, also called quicksilver.

This is the name for a substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. Water and carbon dioxide are examples. For 10 points, give this term, contrasted with a mixture.

Atoms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons are called these. They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are examples, and the latter is used in dating ancient objects. For 10 points, name these variants of an element.

Dmitri Mendeleev arranged elements by increasing atomic mass in the first widely accepted version of this chart. He left gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered. For 10 points, name this chart whose columns are called groups.
This type of reaction gives off heat to its surroundings, making the surroundings warmer. Burning wood is an example. For 10 points, name this kind of reaction, the opposite of endothermic.
This number is the count of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It identifies the element and sets the order of the modern periodic table. For 10 points, name this number, symbolized Z.

The elements in Group 18 of the periodic table are known by this name. They have full outer electron shells, so they rarely react. Helium, neon, and argon belong to this group. For 10 points, give this name.

The compound with the formula H2SO4 is an example of this type of substance. Such substances taste sour, turn blue litmus paper red, and release hydrogen ions in water. For 10 points, name this type of substance, which reacts with bases.
Positively charged ions of this type are formed when an atom loses electrons. Sodium becomes one by losing a single electron. For 10 points, name these ions, which are attracted to the cathode.

This metal is the main component of steel and has the symbol Fe. It rusts when it reacts with oxygen and water. Hemoglobin in your blood contains atoms of this element at the center of its heme groups. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 26.
In this type of mixture, one substance is evenly dissolved in another, such as salt in water. The dissolved substance is called the solute. For 10 points, name this kind of homogeneous mixture.

This number, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd, is the number of particles in one mole of a substance. It lets chemists convert between the mass of a sample and the count of its atoms or molecules. It is named for an Italian scientist. For 10 points, name this constant.

This gas makes up about 78 percent of Earth's atmosphere. It has the symbol N2, and its two atoms are joined by a very strong triple bond. It is used to make fertilizers and ammonia, and liquefied forms of it are used as a coolant. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 7.

The Law of Conservation says that this quantity is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, so a balanced equation has the same total of it on both sides. Antoine Lavoisier established this law. It is measured in grams or kilograms. For 10 points, name this quantity, which is different from weight.
This scientist proposed a model of the atom in 1913 in which electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels. Later quantum models replaced it. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist.

This rule says that atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons until they have eight electrons in their outermost shell. It explains why sodium forms Na plus and chlorine forms Cl minus. For 10 points, name this rule.
These organic compounds, such as methane, ethane, and propane, contain only carbon and hydrogen. Fossil fuels such as natural gas are mostly made of them. For 10 points, name these compounds.
This law relates the pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature, showing that they are inversely proportional. It is named for an Anglo-Irish chemist. For 10 points, name this gas law.
In 1869 this Russian chemist published a periodic table and predicted properties of undiscovered elements such as germanium. For 10 points, name this scientist who created a famous periodic table.

This process is used to separate the components of a liquid mixture by their different boiling points. The vapor is cooled and condensed in a condenser. For 10 points, name this separation technique used to purify water and refine crude oil.

This is the term for the weighted average of the masses of an element's naturally occurring isotopes, measured in unified units. It appears under each element's symbol on the periodic table and is usually not a whole number. For 10 points, give this term.

A catalyst speeds up a reaction by lowering this quantity, the minimum energy that colliding particles need in order to react. On a reaction energy diagram it is the height of the hill between reactants and products. It is symbolized Ea. For 10 points, name this energy barrier.

text: This type of rock forms when magma or lava cools and hardens. Granite forms slowly underground, while basalt forms quickly at the surface. Obsidian is a glassy example of it. For 10 points, name this rock type, which is different from sedimentary and metamorphic rock.

This type of rock forms when layers of sand, mud, and shell fragments are pressed and cemented together over time. Sandstone, limestone, and shale are examples, and fossils are usually found in it. For 10 points, name this rock type.

This is the name of the innermost region of the Earth, made mostly of iron and nickel. It is divided into a liquid outer part and a solid inner part, and it is hotter than the surface of the Sun. For 10 points, name this layer at the center of the planet, below the mantle.

The movement of this kind of large, slowly moving piece of Earth's lithosphere causes earthquakes and mountain building. Examples include the Pacific and North American ones. For 10 points, name these rigid pieces of the crust and upper mantle.

This is the name for a giant ocean wave caused by an underwater earthquake or landslide. It can travel across an entire ocean and flood coastlines. For 10 points, name this kind of wave, often called a "tidal wave" in error.
This process of water moving continuously between oceans, air, and land involves evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. For 10 points, name this cycle that moves Earth's water.

These visible masses are made of countless tiny water droplets or ice crystals that formed when water vapor condensed. Cumulus, stratus, and cirrus are types of them. For 10 points, name these white or gray features of the sky that can produce rain and snow.

The Earth is tilted on its axis by about 23.5 degrees, which is the cause of these four periods of the year. Spring, summer, autumn, and winter are examples. For 10 points, name these periods of changing weather and daylight.
This is the name for the layer of gases surrounding Earth that is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. It includes the troposphere, where weather happens. For 10 points, name this envelope of gases.
This scale from 1 to 10 ranks the hardness of minerals by whether one can scratch another. Talc is 1 and diamond is 10. For 10 points, name this scale named for a German mineralogist.

This kind of fuel formed from the remains of ancient plants and animals that were buried and heated for millions of years. Coal, oil, and natural gas are examples. For 10 points, name this kind of nonrenewable fuel.
Volcanoes in the Ring of Fire are found around the edge of this largest ocean. The Mariana Trench lies beneath this ocean. For 10 points, name this ocean that lies between Asia and the Americas.

This type of seismic wave is the first to arrive at a seismograph after an earthquake. It is a compressional wave that can travel through solids and liquids. For 10 points, name this wave, designated by the letter P.

This is the name of the process in which rock is broken down into smaller pieces by wind, water, ice, or plants. It differs from erosion because the pieces are not moved away. For 10 points, name this process.

This scale ranks the strength of earthquakes by the energy they release. Each whole number increase means about 32 times more energy. For 10 points, name this scale, used today in place of the older Richter scale.

This is the name of the supercontinent that existed about 250 million years ago and later broke apart. Alfred Wegener used its fit as evidence for continental drift. For 10 points, name this landmass whose name means "all land."

Stalactites and stalagmites form in these underground chambers, which are often found in limestone. Carlsbad in New Mexico and Mammoth in Kentucky are famous ones. For 10 points, name these natural underground spaces.

This is the name of the point on Earth's surface directly above the place underground where an earthquake starts. Seismologists find it by comparing the arrival times of waves at three or more stations. It is located right above the focus. For 10 points, give this term.
This is the name of the boundary between the crust and the mantle. It is named for a Croatian seismologist who discovered it in 1909. For 10 points, give this name, often shortened to the Moho.

Warm, moist air rising along a boundary where it meets cooler air forms these kinds of boundaries between air masses. They bring clouds and rain and are drawn on weather maps with colored lines. For 10 points, name these boundaries.

This is the term for the preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms, such as bones, shells, or footprints. They are most often found in sedimentary rock. For 10 points, name these relics of past life.

The Colorado River carved this enormous canyon in northern Arizona. It is about 277 miles long and exposes nearly two billion years of rock layers, and it is a national park visited by millions each year. For 10 points, name this canyon.
This is the name of the soil layer, also called the A horizon, that is rich in humus and supports plant growth. It lies above the subsoil. For 10 points, name this uppermost layer of soil.

This is the name of the movement of sediment by a river, glacier, or wind from one place to another. It differs from weathering because rock pieces are carried away. For 10 points, name this process that wears down Earth's surface.

This is the name of the layer of the atmosphere between about 12 and 50 kilometers up that contains the ozone layer. Weather balloons and airliners often reach its lower part. For 10 points, name this layer above the troposphere.
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is an example of this type of plate boundary, where plates move apart and new crust forms. For 10 points, name this type of boundary, the opposite of convergent.

The mineral calcite is the main component of these two rocks, which are used in building and sculpture. One of them is metamorphic and made from the other, which is sedimentary. For 10 points, name the sedimentary one, found in many caves.

This type of volcano has gently sloping sides built up from runny lava flows. Mauna Loa in Hawaii is an example. For 10 points, name this broad type of volcano that is named for a protective plate of armor.
This is the name of the global ocean current that warms Western Europe. It flows north from the Gulf of Mexico along the east coast of the United States. For 10 points, name this current.

text: This is the name for a huge, slow-moving mass of ice that forms on land from compacted snow. Valleys in places such as Yosemite were carved by these, and Greenland holds an enormous ice sheet of this kind. For 10 points, name this river of ice.

This is the name for a testable explanation or educated guess that scientists make before running an experiment. It is often written as an "if, then" statement. For 10 points, name this step of the scientific method that comes after asking a question and doing background research.

This is the factor in an experiment that the scientist deliberately changes to see what effect it has. It is plotted on the x-axis of a graph. For 10 points, name this kind of variable, contrasted with the dependent variable.

This English scientist developed the first successful smallpox vaccine in 1796 using material from cowpox sores. For 10 points, name this physician, who is often called the founder of immunology and vaccination.

This is the type of microorganism that includes Escherichia coli and Streptococcus. These single-celled prokaryotes can cause strep throat, but antibiotics such as penicillin can kill many of them. For 10 points, name these microbes, whose name ends in the plural "-ia."

This device is used by scientists to see tiny objects such as cells and microorganisms. It uses lenses to magnify and was improved by Anton van Leeuwenhoek in the 1600s. For 10 points, name this instrument.

This is the name for any material that is used by the body for energy, growth, and repair, such as vitamins, minerals, proteins, and carbohydrates. For 10 points, name these substances that are obtained from food.

This is the name of the human organ that is protected by the skull and controls thinking, memory, and movement. It is made up of the cerebrum, the cerebellum, and a stem that joins the spinal cord. Neurons in it send signals through the nervous system. For 10 points, name this organ at the top of the central nervous system.

This is the name for the type of energy that comes from the Sun and can be captured by panels made of silicon cells. It is a renewable resource. For 10 points, name this kind of energy, which produces electricity from photovoltaic cells.
This Polish-French scientist discovered the elements polonium and radium. She won Nobel Prizes in both Physics and Chemistry. For 10 points, name this scientist who coined the term "radioactivity."

Scientists called paleontologists study these preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms, such as bones, shells, and footprints, usually found in sedimentary rock. Dinosaur bones and trilobite shells are examples. For 10 points, name these relics of past life.

This is the name for the variety of living things in an ecosystem or on Earth. It includes the diversity of species, genes, and ecosystems. For 10 points, give this word that combines "bio" with a word for variety.

This is the name for the process in which a substance in a food, like iron or calcium, is taken into the blood from the small intestine. Villi increase the surface area of the small intestine for it. For 10 points, name this process.
This vitamin, which is made in the skin when it is exposed to sunlight, helps the body absorb calcium. A lack of it causes rickets in children. For 10 points, name this vitamin, abbreviated D.

This disease was the target of a global vaccination campaign led by the World Health Organization that ended in 1980 with its eradication. Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine against it. For 10 points, name this viral disease that caused scarring marks and killed millions.
This is the name for the unit of heredity found on a chromosome that carries the code for a protein. Gregor Mendel called them "factors." For 10 points, name these segments of DNA.
This Scottish bacteriologist discovered penicillin in 1928 after noticing mold killed bacteria on a petri dish. For 10 points, name this scientist who shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine.

In this layer of a food chain, the organisms eat the primary consumers. Hawks and snakes that eat mice are examples. For 10 points, name this category of consumers, third in a food chain starting with producers.

This is the name for the bone that forms the upper arm and connects the shoulder to the elbow. It is the longest bone of the arm, and its lower end meets the radius and ulna. For 10 points, name this long bone, whose name sounds like a word for being funny.

This is the name for the substance in the blood that fights infections caused by germs and is made by white blood cells. The body makes it in response to antigens. For 10 points, name this Y-shaped protein.
This is the largest organ of the human body. It protects against germs, regulates temperature, and is composed of the epidermis and dermis. For 10 points, name this organ that covers the body.

This is the name of the field of science that studies how living things interact with each other and their surroundings. The term was coined by Ernst Haeckel. For 10 points, name this branch of biology.

This Russian physiologist discovered conditioned reflexes by training dogs to salivate at the sound of a bell. For 10 points, name this scientist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

This German bacteriologist identified the bacteria that cause tuberculosis and cholera in the 1880s. His set of criteria for linking a germ to a disease is called his postulates. For 10 points, name this scientist.
This is the term for the maximum number of individuals of a species that an environment can support over time. Food, water, and space limit it. For 10 points, name this ecological concept.

This Hungarian physician in the 1840s showed that handwashing in a Vienna hospital dramatically cut deaths from childbed fever. For 10 points, name this doctor, who was largely ignored in his lifetime.
This type of study uses a control group that gets a fake treatment with no active ingredient. The patients do not know whether they got the real drug. For 10 points, name this fake treatment.

This kind of ecosystem process involves bacteria that convert nitrogen gas into ammonia usable by plants. Legumes such as clover and beans host the bacteria in root nodules. For 10 points, name this process of making nitrogen available in the nitrogen cycle.

This ecological term names a species whose presence has an unusually large effect on its ecosystem compared with its numbers. Sea otters that protect kelp forests are an example. For 10 points, give this term.

This is the term for an organism that harms another organism, its host, while living on or in it. Tapeworms and ticks are examples. For 10 points, name this type of symbiotic relationship in which one species benefits at another's expense.

This French scientist developed pasteurization and a rabies vaccine. His experiments in the 1860s supported germ theory. For 10 points, name this man whose name is used for heating milk to kill bacteria.

text: This quantity is the rate at which an object changes its position, and it includes a direction when treated as a vector. Its SI unit is the meter per second. Cars display its magnitude on a speedometer. For 10 points, name this quantity, which is distance divided by time.

This scientist formulated three laws of motion and a law of universal gravitation. He published the Principia in 1687. A unit of force is named for him. For 10 points, name this English physicist, who supposedly was inspired by a falling apple.

This force opposes the relative motion of two surfaces in contact. It is the reason a sliding book eventually comes to rest on a table. It produces heat when you rub your hands together. For 10 points, name this force, which is reduced by lubricants like oil.

This is the SI unit of energy and work, equal to one newton-meter. It is named for an English brewer who studied heat and mechanical equivalence. A watt is one of these per second. For 10 points, name this unit, abbreviated J.

This is the tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion. Newton's first law is sometimes named for it. A passenger lurches forward when a car brakes suddenly because of it. For 10 points, name this property, which is greater for more massive objects.

This is the rate at which velocity changes with time. Near Earth's surface, falling objects have this value of about 9.8 meters per second squared when air resistance is ignored. Newton's second law relates force, mass, and this quantity. For 10 points, name this quantity.

This type of energy is possessed by an object because of its motion. It equals one half mass times velocity squared. A roller coaster has the most of it at the bottom of a hill. For 10 points, name this form of energy, contrasted with potential energy.

This Italian scientist used a telescope to discover four large moons of Jupiter. Legend says he dropped objects from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. He was tried by the Inquisition for supporting heliocentrism. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This is the bending of a light ray as it passes from one medium into another, such as from air into water. It makes a straw in a glass of water appear broken. Lenses work because of it. For 10 points, name this phenomenon, distinct from reflection.

This subatomic particle carries a negative charge and orbits the nucleus of an atom. It was discovered by J. J. Thomson in 1897. The flow of these particles through a wire makes up an electric current. For 10 points, name this particle.

This is the SI unit of power, equal to one joule per second. A common lightbulb is rated in units of this name. It honors the Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine. For 10 points, name this unit, abbreviated W.

This quantity is the product of an object's mass and its velocity. It is conserved in collisions in an isolated system. A heavy truck moving slowly can have the same amount as a fast bullet. For 10 points, name this vector quantity.

This is the type of heat transfer in which warm fluid rises and cool fluid sinks, setting up a circulating current. It drives the movement of air in weather systems. It occurs in a pot of boiling water. For 10 points, name this process, distinct from conduction and radiation.

This law states that the current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across it when temperature is constant. It is often written V equals I times R. It was formulated by a German physicist in 1827. For 10 points, name this law relating voltage, current, and resistance.

This Greek scholar discovered that an object submerged in a fluid feels an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. According to legend, he shouted "Eureka" after having this insight in a bath. For 10 points, name this scholar, whose principle explains why ships float.

This is the effect in which the observed frequency of a wave changes when the source and observer move relative to one another. It explains why an ambulance siren sounds higher as it approaches. It is used in radar speed guns. For 10 points, name this effect, named for an Austrian physicist.

This is the SI unit of frequency, equal to one cycle per second. It is named for a German physicist who first demonstrated radio waves. Radio stations are labeled in kilo- and mega- versions of it. For 10 points, name this unit.

This type of simple device consists of a mass hanging from a fixed point and swinging back and forth. Galileo noted that for small swings its period depends on its length rather than the size of the swing. Grandfather clocks use one. For 10 points, name this device.

This English scientist discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831 and invented an early electric motor. He gave public Christmas lectures at the Royal Institution, including one on the chemical history of a candle. For 10 points, name this scientist for whom a "cage" that blocks electric fields is named.
This is the SI unit of pressure, equal to one newton per square meter. It is named for a French mathematician and physicist who studied fluids and wrote Pensees. For 10 points, name this unit.

Newton showed that a glass triangular object can split white light into a spectrum, a process called dispersion. For 10 points, name this transparent object that separates sunlight into colors, as in an album cover by Pink Floyd.

In physics, this quantity is calculated as force times the distance moved in the direction of the force. Its units are joules. Lifting a box onto a shelf requires this to be done against gravity. For 10 points, name this quantity, which is transferred to an object when a force moves it.

This is the term for the lowest possible temperature, equal to zero kelvin. At this temperature particles have minimal thermal motion. It corresponds to about minus 273 degrees Celsius. For 10 points, name this temperature.

Light is made of tiny packets of energy called these. Albert Einstein used this concept to explain the photoelectric effect. Their energy is proportional to the frequency of the light. For 10 points, name these particles of light.

This type of lens is thicker in the middle than at the edges and focuses parallel light rays to a point. Magnifying glasses and the lens in a camera are examples. The curved shape is called convex. For 10 points, name this kind of lens, which can form real images.

In this device, an alternating current in a primary coil induces a voltage in a secondary coil sharing an iron core. The ratio of turns in the coils determines whether voltage is stepped up or stepped down. Power companies use these to send electricity across long distances at high voltage. For 10 points, name this device.

This scientist's equation E equals m c squared relates mass and energy. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for explaining the photoelectric effect. He also developed the theories of special and general relativity. For 10 points, name this German-born physicist.

This principle states that the pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout it. Hydraulic lifts and car brakes make use of it. It is named for the same Frenchman as the SI unit of pressure. For 10 points, name this principle, a law of fluid statics.

This property of a wave describes the maximum displacement from its rest position. For a sound wave, greater values correspond to louder sounds, and for light, to greater brightness. It is not the same as wavelength. For 10 points, name this property, half of the peak-to-peak height of a transverse wave.

This is the name for the region around a magnet in which other magnets and magnetic materials feel a force. Iron filings sprinkled near a bar magnet trace out its lines. Earth has one that protects the planet from the solar wind. For 10 points, name this kind of field.

text: This object contains about 99.8 percent of the mass of the solar system. Its energy comes from nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core. Sunspots and solar flares are features of its surface and atmosphere. For 10 points, name this star at the center of the solar system.

This is the largest planet in the solar system. It has a Great Red Spot, a storm larger than Earth, and dozens of moons including Io and Europa. It is a gas giant between Mars and Saturn in distance from the Sun. For 10 points, name this planet.

This planet is known for a spectacular system of rings made mostly of ice particles. It is a gas giant with a large moon named Titan. Galileo first saw the rings through a telescope but could not tell what they were. For 10 points, name this sixth planet from the Sun.

This planet is called the "Red Planet" because of iron oxide on its surface. It has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, and the largest volcano in the solar system. Rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance have explored it. For 10 points, name this fourth planet from the Sun.

This planet is the hottest in the solar system because a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat. It rotates backward compared with most planets and is often called Earth's twin due to its similar size. It is the brightest planet in the evening and morning sky. For 10 points, name this second planet from the Sun.

This is the smallest planet in the solar system and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no atmosphere and extreme temperature swings between day and night. It is named for the Roman messenger god. For 10 points, name this planet.

This planet is the farthest from the Sun among the eight planets. It was discovered in 1846 after its position was predicted from irregularities in the orbit of Uranus. It is a blue ice giant with the moon Triton. For 10 points, name this planet.

This kind of event occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun and blocks the Sun's light. During a total one, the corona becomes visible. Viewers must wear special glasses to watch the partial phases. For 10 points, name this event.

This is the distance that light travels in one year, roughly nine and a half trillion kilometers. Astronomers use it to describe distances between stars. Despite its name, it measures distance rather than time. For 10 points, name this unit.

This is a small icy body that develops a glowing tail when it nears the Sun. Its nucleus is often described as a dirty snowball. Halley's is the most famous periodic example. For 10 points, name this object, whose tail always points away from the Sun.

This is the galaxy that contains the Sun and the solar system. It is a barred spiral galaxy with a dense center and several arms. From Earth, it appears as a hazy band of light across the night sky. For 10 points, name this galaxy.

Humans use this instrument to magnify distant objects in the sky. Galileo used an early version in 1609 and 1610, and the Hubble is a famous orbiting one. Refracting and reflecting types use lenses and mirrors, respectively. For 10 points, name this instrument.

This region of the solar system lies mostly between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. It contains millions of rocky bodies, including the dwarf planet Ceres, which is its largest member. The gravity of Jupiter kept them from forming a planet. For 10 points, name this region.

This star is almost directly above Earth's north pole, so it appears to stay still while others circle it. It is the end of the handle of the Little Dipper. Navigators have used it to find north. For 10 points, name this star, also called the North Star.

This kind of event occurs when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon and the Moon moves into Earth's shadow. The Moon may look reddish during totality. It can only happen at full moon. For 10 points, name this event.

This is a pattern of stars as seen from Earth that cultures have named after figures like hunters and animals. Orion and Ursa Major are examples. The International Astronomical Union recognizes 88 of them. For 10 points, name this term for such a star grouping.

This event is the explosion that ends the life of a massive star, briefly outshining its entire galaxy. Tycho Brahe observed one in 1572. The Crab Nebula is the remnant of one seen in 1054. For 10 points, name this kind of stellar explosion.

This is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape beyond its event horizon. Many form when massive stars collapse. A supermassive one lies at the center of the Milky Way. For 10 points, name this object.

This is an object that was reclassified as a dwarf planet by the International Astronomical Union in 2006. Clyde Tombaugh discovered it in 1930. The New Horizons spacecraft flew past it in 2015. For 10 points, name this world, once the ninth planet.

This is the name of the streak of light seen when a small piece of space debris burns up in Earth's atmosphere. People often call it a shooting star. If the object reaches the ground, it is called a meteorite. For 10 points, name this phenomenon.

This American astronaut commanded Apollo 11 and was the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969. He said the words "one small step for man." He was a Navy pilot before joining NASA. For 10 points, name this astronaut.

This Polish astronomer proposed in De revolutionibus orbium coelestium that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun. His heliocentric model challenged the older Ptolemaic system. For 10 points, name this scientist, who published his book in 1543.

These are periodic rises and falls of sea level on Earth caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon. Most coasts have two high ones per day. They are strongest during spring ones at new and full moon. For 10 points, name this phenomenon.

This large orbiting laboratory is operated by several space agencies, including those of the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada. It has been continuously occupied by crews since 2000. It orbits Earth about every 90 minutes. For 10 points, name this station.

This 1957 satellite launched by the Soviet Union was the first artificial object to orbit Earth. Its beeping radio signals could be heard by amateur radio operators. Its launch began the space race. For 10 points, name this satellite, whose name means "traveling companion."

This orbiting observatory, launched from the space shuttle Discovery in 1990, was named for the astronomer who showed that other galaxies exist. A flaw in its mirror was fixed in 1993. For 10 points, name this space telescope.

This storm on Jupiter has been observed for centuries and is a giant anticyclone. It is larger than Earth in diameter. It is located in the planet's southern hemisphere. For 10 points, name this feature, whose color gives it its name.

These are colorful lights that appear in the sky near the polar regions when charged particles from the Sun hit gases in the atmosphere. In the north they are called the northern lights. For 10 points, name this phenomenon, named for the Roman goddess of dawn.

This planet was discovered by William Herschel in 1781. It has an axis of rotation tilted about 98 degrees, so it rotates nearly on its side. Its moons are named for characters in works by Shakespeare and Pope. For 10 points, name this seventh planet from the Sun.

text: This theorem states that in a right triangle, the sum of the squares of the two legs equals the square of the longest side. The 3-4-5 triangle is the best-known example of it. It is written a squared plus b squared equals c squared. For 10 points, name this theorem, attributed to a Greek philosopher.

This irrational number is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. It begins 3.14159 and its decimal expansion never repeats. Many people celebrate a holiday on March 14 in its honor. For 10 points, name this constant, represented by a Greek letter.

This kind of whole number greater than one has exactly two positive divisors, itself and one. Two is the only even one. The numbers 3, 5, 7, and 11 are examples. For 10 points, name these numbers, which are the building blocks of multiplication.

This is the longest side of a right triangle and lies opposite the right angle. Its length can be found from the other two sides using the Pythagorean theorem. The word comes from Greek words meaning "stretching under." For 10 points, name this side.

In a set of numbers arranged from least to greatest, this value is the one in the middle. If there is an even number of values, it is the average of the two middle ones. It is often used for incomes because it is not affected by extreme values. For 10 points, name this measure of center, distinct from the mean and the mode.

This quantity measures the steepness of a line and is often described as rise over run. In the equation y equals m x plus b, it is the letter m. A horizontal line has a value of zero for it. For 10 points, name this quantity.

This operation undoes squaring. Its symbol is a radical sign, and the one of 49 is 7. The one of 2 is an irrational number about equal to 1.414. For 10 points, name this operation, which finds a number that multiplied by itself gives the original.

This number is the additive identity, because adding it to any number leaves that number unchanged. Multiplying any number by it gives itself. Dividing by it is undefined. For 10 points, name this number, which Indian mathematicians treated as a number in its own right.

In the expression 5 cubed, the number 3 is called this. It tells how many times to use the base as a factor. Scientific notation uses powers of ten. For 10 points, give this term, also called a power.
This six-sided polygon is the shape of the cells in a honeycomb. A regular one has interior angles of 120 degrees. Snowflakes have six-fold symmetry based on it. For 10 points, name this polygon.
This is the distance from the center of a circle to any point on it. It is half the diameter. The area of a circle is pi times the square of this length. For 10 points, name this line segment.

This Greek mathematician wrote the Elements, a textbook of thirteen books on geometry and number theory. He gave a famous proof that there are infinitely many primes. He is often called the "father of geometry." For 10 points, name this Alexandrian mathematician.

In this sequence, each term after the first two is the sum of the previous two: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. It appears in the arrangement of seeds in sunflowers and in spiral shells. It was introduced to Europe in Liber Abaci in 1202. For 10 points, name this sequence, named for an Italian mathematician.

In this triangular array, each entry is the sum of the two entries above it. Its rows give the coefficients in the binomial expansion. The numbers 1, 3, 3, 1 form its fourth row. For 10 points, name this array, named for a French mathematician.

This is the U-shaped graph of a quadratic function. A thrown ball follows a path of this shape, and satellite dishes have a cross-section of this shape. Its highest or lowest point is called the vertex. For 10 points, name this curve.

This French philosopher and mathematician introduced the coordinate plane that bears his name. He wrote "I think, therefore I am." His analytic geometry linked algebra to geometry. For 10 points, name this man.

This German mathematician, called the "Prince of Mathematicians," supposedly summed the integers from 1 to 100 as a schoolboy. He proved the fundamental theorem of algebra. A unit of magnetic field is named for him. For 10 points, name this mathematician, whose first name was Carl Friedrich.

This Swiss mathematician introduced the notation f of x for functions and the use of the letter e for the base of natural logarithms. He solved the Konigsberg bridge problem, founding graph theory. For 10 points, name this man, whose last name is pronounced "oiler."

This operation applied to a positive integer n means multiplying all the whole numbers from 1 up to n. It is written with an exclamation point. Five of these equals 120. For 10 points, name this operation, which is used to count arrangements.

This branch of mathematics measures how likely an event is to occur, using numbers between zero and one. Flipping a fair coin and getting heads has a value of one half. For 10 points, name this field, whose study began with gambling problems discussed by Pascal and Fermat.

In statistics, this measure of center is the value that appears most often in a data set. A data set can have more than one, or none. For 10 points, name this measure, distinct from the mean and median.
This numeral system uses letters like I, V, X, L, C, D, and M. It was used in ancient Italy and is still found on clock faces and movie copyright dates. For 10 points, name this system of numbers.

This branch of mathematics was developed independently in the seventeenth century by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz. It includes derivatives and integrals. For 10 points, name this field that studies rates of change and accumulation.

This kind of diagram uses overlapping circles to show relationships between sets. The overlap represents elements that belong to both sets. It is named for a British logician. For 10 points, name this diagram.

This one-sided surface can be made by giving a strip of paper a half twist and joining the ends. If you cut it down the middle you get one longer loop. It is named for a German mathematician. For 10 points, name this surface, whose name resembles a "strip."

This number is about 1.618 and is the positive solution to x squared equals x plus one. The ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers approaches it. Artists claim it appears in the Parthenon. For 10 points, name this ratio, represented by the Greek letter phi.

This concept is the idea of something without any bound. The symbol for it resembles a sideways figure eight and was introduced by John Wallis. Georg Cantor showed that there are different sizes of it. For 10 points, name this concept.

A positive integer is this kind of number if it equals the sum of its proper divisors. Six, which equals 1 plus 2 plus 3, is the smallest one. The next is 28. For 10 points, name this kind of number, which Euclid linked to Mersenne primes.

Eratosthenes devised a method named for this object to find primes. One crosses out the multiples of each prime in a list, leaving only the primes. For 10 points, give the household item in the name of this algorithm that "filters" numbers.

These are real numbers that cannot be written as a ratio of two integers. The square root of 2 is the classic example, which a Pythagorean legend says was proved by Hippasus. Their decimals never end or repeat. For 10 points, name this type of number, contrasted with rational ones.

text: This is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task. A recipe is a familiar everyday example of one. Programmers measure how efficient these are by how their running time grows with input size. For 10 points, name this term for a precise procedure, whose name derives from al-Khwarizmi.

Place values in this number system are powers of two, so the decimal number 5 is written as 101. Logic gates in processors operate on its digits. Its two symbols are often represented as true and false. For 10 points, name this number system that uses only 0 and 1.

This is a group of eight bits. It is the usual unit for storing a single character of text. A kilo- version of this unit is about a thousand of them. For 10 points, name this unit of digital information.

This popular programming language was created by Guido van Rossum and named for a British comedy group. It is known for readable code that uses indentation to mark blocks. It is widely used in data science and teaching. For 10 points, name this language, not a snake.

This is the markup language used to structure web pages. It uses tags such as paragraph and heading elements. Cascading Style Sheets are used with it to control appearance. For 10 points, give the four-letter acronym for this language, written by Tim Berners-Lee for hypertext documents.

This is the global network of networks that links billions of computers. It grew out of ARPANET, a project funded by the United States Department of Defense. Email and the World Wide Web both run on it. For 10 points, name this network.

In programming, this structure repeats a block of code until a condition is met or for a set number of times. For and while are common kinds. Without a way to stop it, one of these can run forever. For 10 points, name this structure.

Often called the "brain" of the computer, this component executes program instructions. Its speed is measured in gigahertz, and Intel and AMD make many models. It carries out the fetch, decode, and execute cycle. For 10 points, name this component, abbreviated CPU.

This is the temporary memory a computer uses to store data and programs currently in use. Its contents are lost when the power is turned off. Adding more of it can help a computer run multiple programs. For 10 points, name this kind of memory, abbreviated RAM.

Windows, macOS, and Android are examples of this type of software. It manages hardware, runs applications, and provides a user interface. Without it, a computer cannot run programs like word processors. For 10 points, name this system software, abbreviated OS.

This is the smallest controllable element of a picture on a digital screen. A typical image is made up of a grid of thousands or millions of them. The word is a blend of "picture" and "element." For 10 points, name this unit.

Chrome, Firefox, and Safari are examples of this type of software. It retrieves web pages from servers and displays them. Users type addresses into its address bar. For 10 points, name this kind of program used to surf the web.

This English mathematician proposed the Turing machine and helped break the German Enigma code during World War II. A famous test of machine intelligence is named for him, and the Association for Computing Machinery's highest award bears his name. For 10 points, name this man.

This woman, a daughter of Lord Byron, wrote notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine that include a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers. She is often called an early computer programmer. For 10 points, name this English mathematician.

This British scientist invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN. He wrote the first web browser and server. He proposed HTTP and URLs. For 10 points, name this computer scientist, whose name includes "Berners."

This American rear admiral and computer scientist developed the first compiler and helped create COBOL. She is associated with the story of a moth found in the Harvard Mark II. For 10 points, name this woman, nicknamed "Amazing Grace."

This English mathematician designed the Difference Engine and the Analytical Engine. He is sometimes called the "father of the computer" even though his machines were never completed in his lifetime. Ada Lovelace worked with him. For 10 points, name this inventor.

This is a free, open-source operating system kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991. It powers Android phones, most web servers, and supercomputers. Its mascot is a penguin named Tux. For 10 points, name this operating system kernel.

This is a data structure that stores a collection of items in numbered positions. Most languages start counting positions at zero. Elements are accessed by their index. For 10 points, name this basic structure, a list of values of the same type.

This type of program translates source code written in a language like C into machine code that a processor can run. Grace Hopper wrote an early one. It differs from an interpreter, which runs code line by line. For 10 points, name this program.

This is an organized collection of structured data, typically managed with software and queried with SQL. Banks, libraries, and online stores use them to store records. For 10 points, name this system, where tables hold rows and columns.

This is a type of harmful software designed to damage or gain unauthorized access to computers. Viruses, worms, ransomware, and spyware are all kinds. Antivirus programs try to detect it. For 10 points, name this category of software.

This security system monitors and controls network traffic based on rules and can block unauthorized connections. It may be hardware or software. Its name comes from a wall that stops the spread of a blaze. For 10 points, name this protective system.

The scientist Douglas Engelbart demonstrated this pointing device in 1968 in a presentation later called "The Mother of All Demos." It moves a cursor on screen and has buttons that you click. For 10 points, name this input device whose name comes from a small rodent.
This is a numeric label, such as 192.168.1.1, that identifies a device on a network. Versions 4 and 6 are the main formats. Routers use it to deliver packets. For 10 points, name this address.

This is a data type with only two possible values, true and false. It is named for an English mathematician who developed a system of algebraic logic in 1854. AND, OR, and NOT are operations on it. For 10 points, give this term, named for a nineteenth-century mathematician from Lincoln, England.

This standard assigns numbers to letters and symbols; for example, 65 stands for uppercase A. It uses 7 bits to represent 128 characters. Unicode extended it to cover many more scripts. For 10 points, name this character encoding standard.
alternates: American Standard Code for Information Interchange

text: This observation made by a co-founder of Intel in 1965 states that the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubles about every two years. It has guided the semiconductor industry for decades. For 10 points, name this "law" named for Gordon.

This technique has a function call itself on a smaller version of the same problem until reaching a base case. Computing a factorial and traversing a tree are standard examples. For 10 points, name this programming technique, a joke about which is that you must first understand it.

This model of computing delivers services like storage and software over the internet from remote data centers rather than from a local machine. Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure are major providers. For 10 points, name this model, symbolized by a fluffy weather feature.

text: When this quantity rises, each dollar buys fewer goods, which is why your grandparents remember much cheaper movie tickets. It is commonly measured by the Consumer Price Index. Central banks often aim to keep it low and steady, at around two percent per year. For 10 points, name this general rise in prices over time.

This concept states that people have unlimited wants but only limited resources to satisfy them. It forces every society to answer the questions of what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom. Time, money, and land are all examples of things that have it. For 10 points, name this basic economic problem of limited resources.

When the price of a good rises, producers are usually willing to offer more of it for sale. This relationship is shown by an upward-sloping line on a graph with price on the vertical axis. Together with its counterpart for buyers, it determines market price. For 10 points, name this half of a famous two-curve model, which is the amount of a good that sellers offer.

The law of this concept says that, all else equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity people buy falls. Its curve slopes downward on a graph. Shifts in income, tastes, and the prices of related goods can move the whole curve. For 10 points, name this economic term for how much of a good consumers are willing and able to buy.

A famous example of this idea is that attending college means giving up the wages you could earn at a full-time job. Economists say every choice has one, and it is the value of the next best alternative that you give up. For 10 points, name this concept that is the real price of any decision beyond the money spent.
alternates: cost of the next best alternative

text: It is measured by adding up consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. Simon Kuznets helped develop it in the 1930s. When economists say an economy is growing, they usually mean this figure is rising after adjusting for inflation. For 10 points, name this measure of the total value of goods and services produced within a country, abbreviated G-D-P.

In this kind of market, one firm is the only seller of a product and has no close substitutes. Examples have included a local water utility and, historically, Standard Oil. Because there is no competition, the firm can charge higher prices. For 10 points, name this market structure with a single seller.

Economists often define this event as two consecutive quarters of falling gross domestic product. During it, businesses cut back, unemployment rises, and consumers spend less. A particularly deep and long one is called a depression. For 10 points, name this downturn in economic activity.

This Scottish thinker wrote that a butcher, brewer, and baker serve us out of self-interest rather than benevolence. He described how a division of labor in a pin factory raises productivity. He published a 1776 book on the causes of national prosperity. For 10 points, name this author of The Wealth of Nations.

Established in 1913, this institution has a Board of Governors in Washington and twelve regional banks. It sets monetary policy by buying and selling government securities, and it acts as lender of last resort to banks. For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States, often shortened to the Fed.

This type of tax is placed on goods imported from other countries, which makes foreign products more expensive in the domestic market. The Smoot-Hawley one of 1930 is a famous example. Supporters say it protects domestic industries. For 10 points, name this tax on imports.

People are counted in this category if they are without a job but are actively looking for work. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes a monthly rate for it. A person who has stopped looking, called a discouraged worker, is not counted. For 10 points, name this condition of being jobless, which rose sharply during the Great Depression.

This British economist argued in a 1936 book that governments should increase spending during downturns to boost demand. His ideas influenced the New Deal and the Bretton Woods conference. He wrote The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money. For 10 points, name this economist whose name labels a school of thought.

David Ricardo illustrated this principle with the example of wine from Portugal and cloth from England. It holds that countries should specialize in what they produce at the lowest opportunity cost, even if another country is better at everything. For 10 points, name this principle that explains the gains from trade.

Owning a share of this means owning a small piece of a corporation. Its price is shown on tickers on exchanges like the Nasdaq. Owners may receive dividends. For 10 points, give this term for a unit of ownership in a company, which is bought and sold on markets.

This is the price of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage of the amount borrowed. When it falls, mortgages and car loans become cheaper and spending tends to rise. The Federal Reserve influences it through its federal funds target. For 10 points, name this cost of a loan.

This decade-long period began after the stock market crash of 1929. Unemployment in the United States reached about a quarter of workers, and thousands of banks failed. Franklin Roosevelt responded with the New Deal. For 10 points, name this worst economic downturn of the twentieth century.

OPEC members are often cited as an example of this market structure, in which a few large firms dominate, so each one's choices affect the others. Airlines and wireless carriers in many countries show it. Game theory, including the prisoner's dilemma, is often used to analyze it. For 10 points, name this market with only a handful of sellers.

Congress and the President use this tool by changing taxes and government spending. During a recession, a government might cut taxes or build highways to stimulate the economy. The other main tool, controlled by the central bank, is monetary policy. For 10 points, name this type of policy involving a government's budget.

This University of Chicago economist advocated that the money supply grow at a steady rate. He won the 1976 Nobel Prize and wrote Capitalism and Freedom. He was a leading monetarist and critic of Keynes. For 10 points, name this economist.

This is the opposite of inflation: a general fall in prices across the economy. It can seem good for shoppers, but it can cause people to delay purchases and make debts harder to repay. Japan struggled with it for years in the 1990s. For 10 points, name this decline in the general price level.

Economists measure this property using a ratio of the percentage change in quantity to the percentage change in price. Gasoline is considered to have low values of it in the short run, while luxury goods have high ones. When it is less than one, the good is described as inelastic. For 10 points, name this property that describes how sensitive buyers are to price changes.

A country has this when the value of its imports exceeds the value of its exports. The United States has had one with China for decades. It is part of the current account. For 10 points, name this imbalance in international trade, the opposite of a surplus.

This occurs in a year when a government spends more money than it collects in revenue. It is financed by borrowing, and the total of past ones forms the national debt. For 10 points, name this gap between spending and revenue in a government budget.

In this system of exchange, people trade goods or services directly without using money. It required a double coincidence of wants, which made trading difficult and led to the invention of currency. For 10 points, name this practice of swapping one good for another.

This word was coined to describe the 1970s American combination of rising unemployment and high inflation, which seemed impossible under older theories. It was triggered partly by oil price shocks from OPEC. For 10 points, name this portmanteau for stagnant growth plus inflation.

On a graph, this is the point where the supply and demand curves cross. At the price named for it, the quantity that buyers want exactly matches the quantity that sellers offer, so there is neither a shortage nor a surplus. For 10 points, give this two-word term, which includes a word meaning balance.

This French-derived word names a person who starts a new business and takes on its financial risk. Steve Jobs and Henry Ford are famous examples. They organize land, labor, and capital to make a product. For 10 points, name this type of business founder.

Adam Smith used this phrase for the way individuals pursuing their own self-interest in free markets end up helping society as a whole, as if guided by something unseen. It appears in The Wealth of Nations and is a key idea of laissez-faire thinking. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase.

This German philosopher co-wrote The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels and also wrote Das Kapital. He criticized capitalism and argued that workers would eventually overthrow the owners of the means of production. For 10 points, name this thinker whose economic theories inspired communism.

This principle states that as you add more of one input, such as workers in a fixed-size factory, each additional unit eventually adds less extra output than the one before. Too many cooks in a small kitchen illustrates it. For 10 points, give this principle of declining marginal output, named for what happens to returns.

text: This scientist trained dogs to salivate at the sound of a bell by repeatedly pairing the bell with food. He was a Russian physiologist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize for work on digestion. For 10 points, name this researcher who discovered classical conditioning.

This Austrian physician founded psychoanalysis and wrote The Interpretation of Dreams. He proposed that the mind has an id, ego, and superego. He used the technique of free association with patients on a couch. For 10 points, name this psychologist.

This process is the mental storing and later retrieving of information. Types include short-term, long-term, and working. Hermann Ebbinghaus studied how quickly forgetting happens on a curve named for him. For 10 points, name this mental ability, which is lost in amnesia.

This psychologist ranked human needs in a pyramid, with physiological needs at the base and self-actualization at the top. He is associated with humanistic psychology. For 10 points, name this American who proposed a hierarchy of needs.

A person with this condition may feel sad, lose interest in activities they once enjoyed, and have changes in sleep and appetite. It is a mood disorder often treated with therapy and medication. For 10 points, name this common mental illness, sometimes called a clinical form of being down.

The Stanford prison experiment was conducted by this psychologist, who also served as president of the American Psychological Association. Participants were assigned roles as guards and prisoners. For 10 points, name this researcher, first name Philip.

In this 1960s study, participants were told to give increasingly strong electric shocks to a learner when he answered incorrectly. Most continued to the highest level because a man in a lab coat told them to. For 10 points, name this Yale study of obedience to authority.

Most vivid ones occur during R-E-M sleep, when the eyes move quickly under the lids. Freud called them the royal road to the unconscious, and he wrote a famous book interpreting them. For 10 points, name these stories and images that the mind produces during sleep.

This part of the brain, shaped like a seahorse, is important for forming new long-term memories. Damage to it caused the famous patient H.M. to be unable to form new memories. For 10 points, name this structure in the limbic system.

This researcher showed children two identical glasses of water, poured one into a taller, thinner glass, and found that young children think the taller one holds more. Tests of this kind of conservation led him to describe stages of development. He was Swiss. For 10 points, name this man.

Psychologists use this term for the way people think they should handle a situation such as stress. Techniques for it include exercise, talking to friends, and deep breathing. For 10 points, name this word, which means managing difficult circumstances.

This term describes the strong emotional bond between an infant and caregiver. John Bowlby proposed a theory about it, and Mary Ainsworth tested it with the Strange Situation procedure. For 10 points, give this term.

The Rorschach test uses these shapes, which are meant to reveal how a person thinks. A person looks at symmetrical inkblots and says what they see. For 10 points, name this kind of test, in which people give open-ended answers to ambiguous images.

B. F. Skinner is known for this kind of learning, in which behavior is shaped by rewards and punishments. He used a box with a lever for rats. For 10 points, name this type of conditioning, named for how the subject acts on its environment.

This term was coined by Leon Festinger for the discomfort felt when a person holds two contradictory beliefs, or acts against their own beliefs. People often change an attitude to reduce it. For 10 points, name this psychological theory.

These disorders are marked by excessive fear or worry. Types include panic disorder, phobias, and generalized forms. For 10 points, name these disorders, which most commonly involve feeling nervous and afraid.

This is the part of the nervous system consisting of the brain and spinal cord. It processes information and sends commands to the rest of the body. For 10 points, give the two-word term, abbreviated C-N-S.

In Freud's theory, this part of the personality is the rational mediator that balances the demands of the id and the superego. It operates on the reality principle. For 10 points, name this part, whose Latin name means I.

This term describes the tendency to do worse at something in front of others, or the opposite. More generally, it names the influence of other people on individuals. For 10 points, name this field of psychology, which studies how people think about and act around other people.
This Swiss psychiatrist founded analytical psychology and developed ideas such as the collective unconscious and archetypes. He broke with Freud in 1913. For 10 points, name this man.

This disorder is often diagnosed in childhood. Symptoms include trouble paying attention, being very active, and acting without thinking. It is abbreviated A-D-H-D. For 10 points, give the full name of this disorder, whose first word is attention.

This 1950s experiment by Solomon Asch showed participants lines of different lengths and had actors give wrong answers. Many subjects went along with the group. For 10 points, name this kind of social pressure, shown in the Asch experiment.

This is the term for a prediction or belief that comes true because a person acts as if it were true. Robert Merton named it. The Pygmalion effect in classrooms is a version. For 10 points, name this kind of prophecy.

This test, developed by Alfred Binet and later revised at Stanford, produces a score meant to measure intelligence. The average score is set at 100. For 10 points, give the abbreviation or full name of this type of score.

This part of the brain, located at the back and below the cerebrum, coordinates balance and fine movement. Damage to it can cause clumsy, shaky walking known as ataxia. Its name is Latin for little brain. For 10 points, name this structure.

This term describes the unlearned tendency, such as sucking in newborns, to respond to certain stimuli. Unlike habits, these are automatic. For 10 points, name this type of inborn response, as when a doctor taps your knee.
This type of therapy, associated with Aaron Beck, helps patients identify and change unhelpful thoughts and behaviors. It is abbreviated C-B-T. For 10 points, name this common therapy.

In his 1960s experiment, Albert Bandura had children watch adults hit an inflatable clown. Children later copied the aggression. For 10 points, name this experiment named for a toy, which showed observational learning.
This is the mental state of being aware of oneself and the surroundings. It is lost during deep anesthesia. For 10 points, name this term, which William James described as a stream.

In medical and psychological trials, a sugar pill given to the control group is an example of this. People who take it often report feeling better simply because they expect to. For 10 points, name this inactive treatment, whose Latin name means I shall please.
